speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: THE LATE JOHN HALL KELLY TRIBUTE TO MEMORY OF CANADA'S FIRST HIGH COMMISSIONER TO EIRE
speechtext:
I have to-day received the following cable from Premier de Valera of
Eire:
I wish to express my sincere sympathy with you and the Canadian government on the death of Mr. Hall Kelly, your distinguished representative in Dublin. He has endeared himself to all who knew him, by his personal qualities, and by his zeal and devotion in fostering close and cordial relations between Canada and Ireland.
I am sure that hon. members of this house will have learned with deep regret of the passing of Canada's first high commissioner to Eire. The career of Mr. John Hall Kelly is a record of industry, charity and devotion to the public interest. With few early advantages, Mr. Kelly gained for himself a high place in his chosen profession of law and success in the businesses in which he was engaged. As a member of the legislature of the province of Quebec, as an appointed member of the legislative council, and as minister without portfolio in the government of Quebec, he gave to his native province long and unselfish service. In him were joined the traditional eloquence of the Irish race and an ever present and kindly interest in the welfare of his fellow men.
Since his arrival in Dublin Mr. Kelly quietly and effectively worked for Canadian-Irish good will. His reports to the government have been of much value and it has been a great satisfaction to myself and my colleagues to note how warmly he has been welcomed by the people of Eire. The tribute which has been paid by Premier de Valera to his personal qualities, his zeal and his devotion is, itself, an indication of the loss which both countries have suffered by Mr. Kelly's passing.

speechtext:
I wish to direct a question to the
Minister of Mines and Resources (Mr. Crerar). Men employed by the Victoria Coal company in the mine known as the Bright-lite at River Hibbert, Nova Scotia, employing 110 men, have been informed by the company and the provincial department of mines that that mine will be closed on April 30 next. In view of the demand for coal at the present time, is there any possibility of keeping the mine operating in this area?

speakeroldname: Hon. T. A. CRERAR (Minister of Mines and Resources):
subtopic: NOTICE OF CLOSING OF BRIGHT-LITE MINE, NOVA SCOTIA, ON APRIL 30 NEXT
speechtext: I do not know of any action which the federal government could take to compel a mine to operate in the province of Nova Scotia. As my hon. friend knows, the mines of Nova Scotia are under the control of the provincial government.

subtopic: NOTICE OF CLOSING OF BRIGHT-LITE MINE, NOVA SCOTIA, ON APRIL 30 NEXT

depend upon the interpretation placed upon the clause which appears in the speech from the throne of the Alberta legislature, more particularly upon the meaning to be attached to the word "this" as it appears in the text. My hon. friend gave me a copy of his question as I came into the house. The clause quoted reads.
The government is pressing strongly for extension of the province's boundaries to include the rich mineral areas of the northwest territories in order that orderly development may be speeded up. We have received with great satisfaction the assurance of the federal government that there appears to be no reason why this should not be done.
If "this" refers to the Alberta government's pressing strongly for an extension of the boundaries, the statement is wholly correct; but if the word "this" is to be interpreted as meaning that there must be an immediate extension further northward of boundaries of Alberta or of any other province, I cannot say that any such undertaking has been given.
What I recall at the moment is this. At the time of the conference between the provinces and the dominion, held a month or two ago, the premier of Alberta and one of his colleagues called upon me to speak about the possible extension of the boundary of Alberta further northward, and wished to know whether this matter could not be taken up at once. Having had one experience with the conference between the dominion and the provinces, my first reply was that I questioned the wisdom of attempting anything of the kind just at this particular time. I had been reminded that there were more pressing matters connected with the war than some of the domestic issues that might be raised. I stated that I doubted whether it would be possible to take up the question of the extension of the boundaries of Alberta to the north without also taking up at the same time, with the governments of Saskatchewan, Manitoba and British Columbia, the question of the extension of their boundaries further north.
I did say that the government at different times had had this matter under consideration but that we had reached no final conclusion with respect to it. However, it was pointed out to me that, in the minds of our friends in Alberta, the addition of the northern lands to the province might be a means of furthering the war effort because of some of the resources that existed there, and I was asked whether I would not arrange to have the matter looked into from that point of view. I replied that

I should certainly be only too pleased to do so, and after the conference I met my colleague, the Minister of Mines and Resources (Mr. Crerar), and asked him to have the officials of his department look into the question of resources to the north of the province of Alberta with a view to considering whether at the present time it would be desirable to take up further with the Alberta government and the governments of other provinces the possibility of an extension of their boundaries to the north. That, I think, accurately represents what was said at the time. As I say, the clause that appears in the speech from the throne is capable of different interpretation. subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Before this resolution, is reported I want to refer to a matter that has not received very much consideration so far. I refer to the great discontent that is prevalent among workers at the present time and to the unsatisfactory employer-labour relations in our war industries. One of the important factors operating against efficiency in our war industries is that neither the government nor employers of labour have tried to secure the confidence and cooperation of organized labour. I have never known of so much discontent among working people as prevails at this time. It arises from the fact that too many industrialists have looked upon war contracts as a lucky bit of business and have failed to realize that they are engaged in a business which concerns not them alone but every Canadian. War contracts are often looked upon as an addition to the ordinary business turnover ratheT than as a ohallenge to our industries to organize the country's resources in an all-out endeavour to destroy the menace to our democratic way of life. After all, I am not so very much surprised that employers look at things as they do. Certainly their outlook and actions at the present time are not democratic. Indeed now in Canada we are seeing a repetition of those things that have been either fatal or nearly fatal to the war effort of our allies in other parts of the world. It was this same attitude on the part of British industrialists, until after the fall of the Chamberlain government, that proved nearly fatal to Great Britain. It was this attitude on the part of the French industrialists that brought about the fall of France; and indeed it is not likely that there has been any change since.
The great majority of the workers in Canada are not only willing but anxious to do their bit in this struggle, but in doing it they want to be considered and accepted as partners in the fight we are engaged in. They want to be consulted on policy and on organization. They object to being considered only good enough to be ordered about. A great deal of time and energy is being frittered away in labour disputes 'that could be used to better advantage in organizing our industries for a successful conclusion to this struggle.
It is almost unbelievable that at this time, when united effort is demanded of everyone, employers should refuse to recognize and cooperate with their employees on a basis of equality. It is even less understandable that the government's policy in planning and organizing the country's war effort should have almost completely left out organized labour. Earlier in this debate, when the matter of conditions in the Malton plant was discussed,

the Minister of Munitions and Supply was asked if he could give any reason for the high labour turnover in that plant, and he said he could not. I asked if he had consulted the workers in the plant, and he replied that he had not, that he had enough grief consulting with the management. It seems to me that in this reply is summed up the whole attitude of both the employers and the government towards the hundreds of thousands of workers in this country who perform the actual labour necessary to our war production. The dissatisfaction in the Malton plant, where in six months there was a labour turnover of from seventy-five to ninety per cent, is not exceptional, but for the turnover figures.
Discontent is rampant in the war industries throughout the country. In the aircraft industry, one of the most important in the war effort, and in this particular plant, there is admittedly a high labour turnover. Yet it never occurred to anyone-not even to those giants, the dollar-a-year men in the Department of Munitions and Supply-to approach the workers in the plant and ask what was the cause of their discontent. It seems to be the studied policy, both on the part of the government and on the part of employers, not to consult labour. The attitude seems to be something like this: Oh, you must not consult labour. It is dangerous. They might get an inflated idea of their importance. Labour must be kept in its place. You give the workers orders; you post notices for them to read, and of course you ask them to subscribe to war savings campaigns, but you must never consult them in regard to the work they are doing, or ask if they have any ideas as to how efficiency and output might be improved.
That seems to be the whole attitude, and before I sit down I am going to prove it. Employers and members of the government must get away from that point of view, otherwise we may very well lose the war; and if we should win it under such policies certainly we will lose the peace. We will have gotten so far away in practice from the principles for which we are supposedly fighting that when peace comes with its own problems we will still be fighting on the labour front. We must realize that to-day efficient production depends upon harmonious labour relations in industry just as much as it depends on efficient management in other directions.
In Great Britain labour is consulted at every turn. If similar conditions prevailed here, there is no reason to doubt that organized labour would act as a check on managerial inefficiency, as it has done in Britain. In my opinion it is necessary to give this recogni-

War Appropriation Bill
tion to labour for two reasons. First, it will improve the general morale so necessary for efficient production, and in that way greatly accelerate the war effort. Second, the democratic objectives of the war make this recognition imperative. Some little time ago we had as a visitor to our country an outstanding labour representative from Great Britain, Sir Walter Citrine. He spoke in many cities across Canada, including Ottawa. I quote a few words from the report of his speech in Ottawa as it appears in the Canadian Congress Journal for February:
The development of collective bargaining in Great Britain is so complete that all but the tiniest fraction of disputes are settled between the employers and the trade unions without any government intervention of any kind.
Then he continued:
After all is said and done before you can have order in industry you must have organization in industry. Before trade unions can control large masses of people those large masses must be members of the unions. In other words, you cannot speak and act for and control a constituency you do not represent.
How impossible it would be for a labour representative from Canada to go to the old country or anywhere else and make a similar statement in regard to Canada!
The situation here is bad from every point of view. Lack of organization is responsible for bad working conditions, and is responsible indeed for the inefficiency prevalent in our war production. I have under my hand dozens of letters complaining of conditions in war industries. Among them I find one from workers in a Montreal plant working on a war contract-The Montreal Construction Supply and Equipment Limited. The chief complaints are, first, that the sanitary conditions in the plant are bad. They say the floors are continually covered with water. To absorb that water sawdust is spread, and the men have to stand in that wet sawdust during the whole of their working time. The second complaint is that at that time the plant was running seven days a week, with considerable overtime-this at a time when many men are idle, and when men are being laid off in other plants engaged in war work.
Then, not only do they work seven days a week, but they work eight-hour shifts, with only fifteen minutes off for lunch. It is claimed that the bolting of meals, unavoidable under these conditions, is having a bad effect on the health of the workers. Furthermore, government wage scales call for 40 cents an hour as a starting wage, increasing to 50 cents an hour after twelve days. But the company, it is said, pays no attention whatsoever to these regulations. Some
men have worked in the plant as long as four months before receiving the stipulated increase.
This company will not tolerate any attempt at labour organization in the plant. I am informed that one of the Catholic trade unions held meetings to which workers in this plant were invited. The company had its stool pigeons at the meeting, and the workers who attended were dismissed the next day. After this episode, the superintendent of the plant, Mr. Lemieux, called the men together as they came off shift and warned them against unions, saying that such unions were made up of crooks and thieves.
We have thousands of police watching for subversive activities among workers and others. But it is treatment of this kind which causes workers to listen, to subversive talk, and to take action which in many cases must ultimately be detrimental to themselves. We will abolish discontent and strife in industry only as we accept the policy, and act upon it, that workers are not just a part of the industrial raw material, but that they are human beings with hopes and aspirations, and they must be considered as such. If we are to have peace and harmony in industry, if we are to have the highest degree of efficiency in production, employers must not only concede the right of the workers to organize but must recognize that because of such organization the workers shall have some say in setting up the wages and the conditions under which they are to work.

Labour has also been invited to give its services in the work of the national war charities funds advisory board, a request which has been gladly complied with. I am not saying that. The editor of the journal, with the approval of the president of the largest labour organization in Canada, is saying it. I have the memorandum submitted to the dominion government by the Canadian Congress of Labour on February 14, 1941. The Canadian congress has this to say:
The congress believes, however, that a greater willingness on the part of the government to consult and cooperate with bona fide labour organizations, in all matters of primary concern to the workers, is imperative, in, the interests -not only of the workers but the people of Canada. In the Montreal Gazette of March 8 there was a report of a board or advisory committee or something of that kind being set up. I got into touch this morning with a representative of the national labour council and he told me he had never heard of it. I quote from the Montreal Gazette of March 8:
Canada is being organized into industrial zones, each with a chairman and committee to work in conjunction with the munitions and supply department "to harness all possible industrial resources to war needs," munitions minister Howe announced to-night.
As I read further down the item I find that this committee, or whatever it is going to be, is carried on by the Canadian Manufacturers' Association and the Canadian Chamber of Commerce with "the approval and support of the Department of Munitions and Supply." I quote further:
In addition, the Canadian Manufacturers' Association and the Canadian Chamber of Commerce will accompany the organization work with a national survey of industrial resources. This survey, to begin this week, will be conducted by a war production committee under joint chairman, L. L. Lang of Kitchener, Ont., and J. D. Johnson of Montreal. Mr. Lang is first vice-president of the C.M.A. and Mr. Johnson is vice-chairman of the executive committee of the C.C.C.
The survey will provide information on labour available, machine tools and other equipment in existing plants.
The national labour supply council was not considered. The member to whom I spoke did not know that such a thing had been contemplated; yet the important factor in a survey of industrial resources is labour. What those who are carrying on this kind of work think of the position of labour is clearly indicated in the phrase, "will provide information on labour available, machine tools and other equipment". Evidently they do not think that labour should have any more place on a committee of this kind than "machine tools and other equipment." Let me tell my hon. friends that this is not the way to build the new social order which the Prime Minister referred to at the time of the ill-fated conference which met in Ottawa on January 14. We shall have to have more cooperation with those who are doing the real work in this war effort, both from the government and from employers, than we have had in the past. Otherwise we are simply riding into trouble.

At this moment nothing is of greater importance in Canada's war effort than shipbuilding. It is of the greatest importance that the government should adopt and announce without further delay a policy with regard to merchant shipping. Perhaps they have that policy ready, perhaps not, but I suggest there should be no further delay in adopting and announcing such a policy. I understand that in Canada we have placed contracts for twenty merchant ships-the minister will correct me if I am wrong-all of them to be built for Great Britain; none to be built for Canada. I understand that none of the twenty keels has been laid.
I doubt whether any hon. member will dispute the importance of shipbuilding. The minister himself clearly indicated the emphasis which he placed upon it when on his return from Great Britain he said in Washington on January 25:
The most important development immediately will be a decided emphasis on merchant ship production and the building of bombing aeroplanes. In one instance we are building transportation and in the other producing machines that can carry themselves over the Atlantic to service. We hope to step up the capacity of all Canadian shipyards. This is one of the first things that must be done.
A month later Lord Beaverbrook made his appeal to Canada. He closed with these words:
Gather together every kind of transport by sea. which will enable us to continue the defence of this island. Seek the whole world for ships; make our sea paths safe during the battle of Britain.

It is impossible to emphasize too strongly what shipping and the shipbuilding industry mean to Canada. We have a great export trade which before the war was practically all carried in ships belonging to other nations. We had practically no merchant fleet. Adequate ocean shipping facilities would be of the greatest importance also in carrying freight between the east and west coasts. For some years before the war a steamship line ran a ship a month to the east and west coasts via the Panama canal, but this service was discontinued when the war broke out, with the result that freight rates have been raised by the railways and a situation has developed which to say the least is very unfair to the provinces on either coast. I suggest to the minister that if we entered into a really large shipbuilding programme, making not only the hulls but also the engines and boilers and auxiliary equipment, on either coast-wherever it may be decided to build the ships-there is no reason why we could not build up a great shipbuilding industry for Canada in the maritime provinces and British Columbia for the years after the war.

A survey recently made by employment services in Vancouver showed that there are at least 1,000 skilled men in British Columbia available for employment in shipyards; that if the labour supply is diluted to include unskilled craftsmen the number of men ready to take shipyard jobs is almost unlimited.
Now I have a word for the Minister of National Defence for Naval Affairs, who gave us a very hopeful and promising-and perhaps optimistic

statement when he spoke in the house on November 19 last. This is what he said, as reported at page 207 of Hansard:
But, Mr. Speaker, we intend to go further. It is our hope that in the Canadian yards we shall be able to build destroyers and perhaps cruisers as well. The building of these craft requires a high degree of skill; they have never before been built in this country. In the early stages of this development we shall require the assistance of skilled men from admiralty dockyards or from private yards in Britain, and we have asked for that assistance.
That was the last the house or the Canadian people heard about this proposal to build destroyers and possibly cruisers. I suggest that the time has now come when the minister should tell us all about it; whether this is another case of the wish being father to the thought, or whether we are in a position to commence building these warships in Canada. I think we must face the fact that it will be impossible for us to have destroyers built in

Great Britain at least during the war and probably after the war. We cannot get started too soon on a policy of building our own destroyers and perhaps our own cruisers. It may be that steps in this direction have been taken, but I think the minister should let us know without further delay.
Summing up my question-or suggestion, whatever it may be called-I think the government should set an objective that will arouse the enthusiasm of the Canadian people in connection with this matter of shipbuilding. Let us go all out on this question. Perhaps the government have an objective now. I suggest that no matter what that objective may be, the government should give consideration to doubling it, because at this time we cannot build too many ships in Canada.

Perhaps I should reply to the hon. member. It sounds so easy to say we should expand our shipbuilding indefinitely, as the hon. member states, but we have done a very considerable job of expanding shipbuilding up to this time. At the beginning of the war one of the first things we did was to fill every shipyard with work to its capacity. It has taken us a great deal of time to build up the shipbuilding organization we have to-day. We started with less than 1,500 men employed in our shipyards. We have been able to bring that figure up to about 20,000 men, and we hope to expand it still further. But to-day, while I do not know about the west coast, I do know about eastern Canada, and I know that every shipyard could use more skilled men if it could get them. The situation is particularly acute in Halifax and Saint John. We have been trying to get the Saint John shipyard on a twenty-four hour basis since the beginning of the war, but we have not been able even to approach that objective. The same is true in Halifax; we are working on short time there. That is the bottleneck of the shipbuilding industry. I could follow the suggestion of my hon. friend, go out to British Columbia and start three or four more shipyards; I know there are promoters ready and anxious to sell stock to the public, in fact are just waiting for that very opportunity, but it would only mean a drain of employees from existing shipyards.
Our shipyards are doing a good job and we have ample work in sight to take care of ithem for a very long period. If it is considered to the advantage of any existing yard to have a further contract, we are in a position to place that contract. At this very time our director of shipbuilding is on the Pacific coast, where he will explore every proposal we have had for additional shipyard

War Appropriation Bill
capacity, in order to determine whether or not in fact we can step up our production of ships by starting additional yards there. I was particularly warned in England about the folly of doing that if it would mean a drain of skilled workmen from other yards. I was told that from their experience it was not wise to start a new yard if the trained personnel had to come from other yards. They expressed the opinion that any yard in Britain could do more work if it had more skilled men, and that unless and until they were sure they had the trained personnel with which to start additional yards, it was not their intention to start them.
I do not think there is a shipyard in Canada, large or small, that has not been offered all the work it can do. The work each yard has taken has depended a good deal on the courage of the operators. We have had some small yards that did not wish to take more than one boat at a time. They wished to take one and finish it before taking a second. We have had others willing to take almost an unlimited number of orders, but there again we see no purpose in placing orders ahead of the time when the yards can actually transform those orders into something more than sheets of paper. In other words, if it is possible to order steel ahead, if it is good business to order steel ahead, they can go ahead and do it. If it is possible to lay a keel, that keel is laid; but, as I say, we are 'trying to develop more shipbuilders here, more skilled men. Steel ships are not things that can be built by men without experience. Shipbuilding is probably one of the most highly skilled businesses we have on hand here at the present time. We are working as hard as we can to develop shipbuilders; we intend to continue doing so, and if the number of shipbuilders available warrants starting additional yards, my hon. friend can be sure that it is our intention to do so.
A word as to the question of destroyers. We have not been idle in this matter. I may tell my hon. friend that we have now obtained our detail sheets; our plate specifications are here, and our plate sizes are here. We have explored the equipment market, and we know exactly where to place orders for equipment. We have been able to obtain a few experienced men from England; the British government was reluctant to spare them but they are on their way here now. We are pushing along the destroyer programme just as quickly as we possibly can, but these things have to be taken up in an orderly way. It would be quite possible to disorganize this whole industry. We could do that; we could encourage everyone to
start yards, but we would reach 'the position where we would be simply churning labour around and building nothing. We are very actively engaged in stepping up the shipbuilding industry of Canada, and just as rapidly as we can step up the ability to construct we will start new projects to be constructed.

They have been looking to Germany as if Germany had a magic way of financing. Hon. members in the house have referred to it, and Social Credit speakers in the country have also referred to Germany's method of financing.
Social Credit's latest recruit, Premier Hep-bum of Ontario, is telling the people of that province that Germany is financing with "rubber money." "With rubber-money, Hitler built an army and seized control of nine capitals of Europe," Mr. Hepburn is reported to have said. Let us consider it for a few moments, but before doing so I should like to picture the background, so that their method of financing may appear in its proper setting.
After the great war Germany issued money so freely that inflation set in. Money became very cheap, and prices of goods very high.

In the year 1924 the old currency was discarded and new currency was set up in Germany. Savings accounts created prior to 1924 were practically wiped out by the inflation. All domestic debts and all debts payable in German currency that matured prior to the introduction of the new currency were practically wiped out. Contracts expressed in the old currency were extinguished. Debts payable in gold or foreign currency as well as unmatured debts payable in German currency were greatly compromised.

Germany was
not overrun during the first great war. Her factories were not damaged; her industry remained intact. Other warring nations had to rebuild much that was destroyed in their countries by the war. Such was not the case in Germany. Her economic activity had been in a measure suspended during the war. After the war she was permitted to carry on as before.
Germany's present military and industrial power is in considerable measure due to the huge loans made to her, largely by the United States, and to some extent by Great Britain, after she stabilized her currency in 1924. Industries proceeded to incur new debts, and to equip their old plants and build new ones with most modern and up-to-date machinery. These borrowings amounted to almost three times the reparation payments Germany was making during the period of prosperity which followed the introduction of the new currency.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
The great
depression of 1929 struck Germany very hard. Unemployment became severe, more severe in proportion to population than in any other European country. The standard of living was reduced to extremely low levels. The standard of morals was lower still. During the course of the depression Germany obtained the benefit of the "Hoover moratorium" on United States and other foreign loans to Germany. When Hitler came into power Germany declared a moratorium on all foreign debts. This enabled her to buy greatly depreciated German bonds at a few cents on the dollar.
On obtaining power on January 30, 1933, Hitler set out to mobilize the military and economic resources of the reich for the purpose of waging war. He developed an organization designed to produce as quickly as possible all that the German people could possibly produce. All this had to be financed. Thorough and far-sighted rearmament is of crucial importance in preparing for a mechanized war. Plans should be laid and the building well under way years before they are used. This has been recognized by all countries in respect of navies which have always been mechanized forces. No country waits until the outbreak of war to build its navy. They build it years before it is needed so as to be ready when war breaks out. The nazis extended this principle to their air and land forces.
With the advent of Hitler, Germany began her rearmament on the basis of a small army of 100,000 men allowed her by the Versailles treaty. Secret rearmament was under way in 1934. It became open and acknowledged in 1935 and began to hit its stride at that time. Flying clubs were formed throughout the country and she became active in building up her air force. At the same time she commenced to mechanize her army for the second world war, so that Germany has, in effect, been on a war economy since 1935 when rearmament got under way on a large scale. Hitler was also preparing for war by striving to make Germany' independent of supplies which might be cut off by enemy activity. In other words, he was striving to make Germany blockade^proof in case of war.
The intensity of the depression created economic conditions for rearmament unparalleled in normal times. When the nazis came to power they found production machinery largely idle and 7,000,000 to 9,000,000 workers unemployed. In the following years it was possible to increase armaments rapidly be-
War Appropriation Bill

cause idle plants and idle men were available in large numbers. As the reich credit society declared in its report for 1936:
Whereas four years ago there were huge reserves of capacity lying idle in the fields of production and investment, to-day the productive possibilities of many industries are not only being utilized to the full, but there is an urgent need for the construction of big new plants.
Hitler regimented agriculture, manufacturing and labour on a national scale. He controlled raw materials and production; he fixed wages and prices; he placed Germany's whole national economy under the direction of military officers whose commands were and are enforced by fines, imprisonment and firing squads. According to an article by Peter F. Drucker in a recent issue of the Saturday Evening Post, there are "2,000,000 persons engaged full time in controlling the economic activities of other persons" in Germany.
As to agriculture, in 1934 elaborate marketing boards were set up. These 'boards undertook to make Germany self-supporting in agricultural products so that she would not have to import products of the farm. They fixed prices on all agricultural products; compulsorily reduced principal and interest rates on farm mortgages; reduced taxes on farms; compelled farmers to sell their products at fixed prices; required farmers to farm in an efficient manner (if a farmer failed to do so they took his farm from him and gave it to someone else who would work it efficiently) ; required a farmer to pass his farm on to his eldest son or other heir. As a consequence, a farmer could not sell his farm or mortgage it to raise money to buy up-to-date machinery. Restrictions were also placed on farm labourers getting work in towns. Labourers were taken from towns and forced to work on farms for little or no wages.
The nazi farm programme has not been a success. There is not a plentiful supply of 'bread. There is a shortage of butter, eggs, cheese, meat, milk and fat products. They had to kill off much of their breeding stock because they lacked feed for it. In the subdued countries Germany confiscated large fodder supplies and shipped them to Germany. Holland and Denmark always import quantities of fodder for their live stock. Owing to the looting by Germany and to imports of fodder being cut off by the blockade, Holland and Denmark were short of fodder and had to slaughter the greater part of their dairy herds. Germany then confiscated the carcases. Some of the smaller countries which have since been overrun anticipated a long war in which they had hoped to remain neutral. They built up

reserves of food. The Dutch built up reserves to last them for four years. The Germans swiftly confiscated and used up these reserve stocks. As a result of Germany's looting, there is a real lack of farm products in the German-controlled countries.
As to industrial control, only those things are produced which the government thinks are necessary and in the quantities deemed necessary. Prices are frozen at the 1936 level. Dividends are limited at from 6 to 8 per cent. Dividends in excess of the authorized limit must be deposited in the reichbank where the funds are held for the account of the shareholders. The funds cannot be withdrawn by the owner but are invested for him in government securities or otherwise under government direction.
The cost of government control and the salaries of the staff required in setting it up and carrying it out are paid by the industry itself. The cost hits small businesses much harder comparatively than it does large businesses. Many small businesses are thus being ruined. Large business, too, has been ruthlessly dealt with. Germany's largest steel enterprise was confiscated by the government and reorganized into the Hermann Goering works. The reason given for confiscating it was that August Thyssen, head of the enterprise, was not cooperating satisfactorily with the nazis. In the countries overrun by Germany she forced the banks to give their money in exchange for reichmarks at a price fixed by the Germans. She is now taking over control of their banks and manufacturing plants.
At a nazi congress held on September 9, 1936, Hitler announced a four-year plan designed, in these words:
In four years to make Germany wholly independent of other countries in all those materials which German capacity, our chemistry, our machine industry, and our mining industry, can produce at home.
Her ambition was to be blockade-proof in case of war.
Germany proceeded to build up new industries by the creation of synthetic ersatz. Without Lorraine, she had to import 84 per cent of her iron ore; as a result of experiments carried out under the four-year plan, a great expansion of production was provided from poor domestic ores. She built up synthetic oil plants, distilling oil from coal; at the commencement of the war more than 50 per cent of her liquid fuel demands were produced from coal. Her leaders say she is now producing 5,000,000 tons of synthetic gasoline a year. This is probably an exaggeration. She

War Appropriation Bill
is believed to be producing a little more than one-half this amount. These plants are favourite targets of British bombers. From coal and lime she produces sufficient synthetic rubber known as "buna" to supply more than one-third of the needs of the army. She produces textiles on a large scale from lumber, straw and other plants as well as from coal, lime, glass and fish. These and other ersatz enterprises were financed in many instances by their competitors in existing industries.
With regard to labour control the economic life in Germany is severely controlled. By reason of this control the nazis are able to carry out effectively, but ruthlessly, their agricultural and rearmament programmes, the four-year plan and the war itself. This control involves the loss of individual freedom and initiative to an extent as great as, if not greater than, that involved in soviet Russia, even though Germany retains the formal capitalistic organization.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: May I ask the hon. member a question? I did not follow that document. He said something just now with relation to labour control. Is what he is giving us a description of labour control in Germany, or in Canada?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
In Germany.
One of the first major actions of the nazis on gaining power was to destroy completely the trade unions and all they stood for. At that time the trade unions were very strong in Germany. Their funds were confiscated; their leaders were killed, imprisoned or driven into exile, and the organizations destroyed.
The unions were replaced by the labour front, which is not a labour organization as we understand labour organizations in this country. The workers have no voice in labour matters. The labour front is a branch of government. Labour trustees appointed by the government are all-powerful officials dealing with labour matters. All workers must belong to the labour front and pay dues to it.
The average worker must pay 16 per cent of his wages for compulsory insurance in the labour front. The labour front also collects sufficient dues from the workers to pay the salaries of 16,000 instructors to train men for jobs requiring skilled workers. They also have to provide winter relief and other funds for the workers.
Wages of workers were reduced to and frozen below the low level of the lowest depression year, 1932, and increases are forbidden, subject only to minor adjustments. Dismissal of workers was prohibited in order to stabilize employment. Food rations have been reduced to the workers since the commencement of
the war. German scientists say a man can do a full day's work on 70 per cent of the food which he consumes under normal conditions. Hence in Germany food is rationed and cut down to 70 per cent of the pre-war level.
The worker under nazi rule is not free to move from one district where there is a scarcity of labour to another where he thinks there is a chance to get better employment. He is not free to give up one job to accept another that will pay him better. An employer is liable to a penalty of $500 if he offers higher wages or otherwise attempts to attract a worker already employed; newspaper advertisements for skilled labour are banned. Hiring and firing are both to a large extent under the control of the government. All skilled workers are registered and are allocated to those jobs which the government deems most necessary.
By the spring of 1938 all employable persons in Germany were mobilized and put to work. Further labour was needed on the Siegfried line. Skilled craftsmen were needed in their factories. As soon as Poland was overrun, the Poles were driven like cattle into Germany and have since been forced to work like slaves. According to the London Economist there have been sent to forced labour in Germany more than 1,000,000 Poles, 100,000 Dutch and 80,000 Slovakians. Mr. John Wheeler-Bennett in an article in New Europe quoted in a recent editorial in the Winnipeg Free Press, says:
German official figures place the number of workers conscripted from the enslaved areas for forced labour in German agriculture and industry at 950.000, including 340,000 from Poland, 160,000 from the low countries, 107,000 from Bohemia and Moravia, and 17,000 from Denmark. These figures are exclusive of prisoners of war, of whom nearly a million are employed, chiefly on the land, but some in activities directly contributing to the nazi war effort, and it was added, somewhat significantly, that a further million conscript workers would be required. According to reports from neutral sources the standards of living of those engaged in forced labour in Germany is so low that many cannot survive, without receiving additional food from home.
The people in the subdued countries are systematically starved in order to increase the surplus that Germany can wring from her conquests. These foreign helots in German factories and on German farms have been driven from their homes by the spectre of starvation. They must work for Germany or starve.
According to German economy, Germany is to be the industrial hub of Europe after the war. Positions which demand initiative and leadership will be reserved for Germans; the more menial tasks will be left to the lesser breeds.
War Appropriation Bill

The Winnipeg Free Press editorial to which I have already referred, further quotes from Mr. Wheeler-Bennett's article in New Europe, from a speech made by Walter Darre, Minister of Agriculture in the reich administration, to nazi officials last May, when a complete nazi triumph for nazi arms appeared to the Germans to be only a few weeks off. Here are Darre's words:
Before autumn sets in we shall be the absolute masters of two continents, with the exception of soviet Russia. It will then be our duty to organize economically the territories gained, which gradually will be included in the German area. We will introduce into our "living space" completely new methods. All soil and industrial property of inhabitants of non-German origin will be confiscated without exception and distributed primarily among the worthy members of the party and soldiers who were accorded honours for bravery in this war. Thus a new aristocracy of German masters (herrenvolk) will be created. This aristocracy will have slaves assigned to it, these slaves to be their property, and to consist of landless, non-German nationals. Please do not interpret the word "slaves" as a parable or as a rhetorical term: we actually have in mind a modern form of mediaeval slavery which we must and will introduce because we urgently need it in order to fulfil our great tasks. These slaves will by no means be denied the blessings of illiteracy; higher education will, in future, be reserved only for the German population of Europe. We have selected this form of slavery for several reasons. The most important reason is that we are abolishing the gold standard and replacing it by work. This work must be as cheap as possible in order that our economic conquest may spread extensively and rapidly. Our future generations must, even in peace time, be educated in such a manner that, in case of necessity, they may be fit to defend strongly and energetically what we acquired. Here too the form of slavery mentioned above will prove its worth. German masters, accustomed to command, and, in case of necessity, to strike inconsiderately where striking is necessary, will be fine pillars to uphold Germany's rule of the world.
From Mr. Wheeler-Bennett's comments on the text supplied by Doctor Darre, the Free Press quotes:
Here in the terse, direct phraseology of nazi rhetoric is the blueprint for that brave new world which Adolf Hitler plans to build upon the ashes and debris of European civilization. This is not the thought of a single man; it is the kind of doctrine currently discussed by the inner circles of the nazi party.
Last Wednesday's Lethbridge Herald, in an editorial, tells of the cruelties and indignities to be visited upon the British if Hitler wins. It quotes a nazi agent who writes:
As soon as we beat England we shall make an end of you English once and for all. Ablebodied men and women will be exported as slaves to the continent. The old and the weakly will be exterminated.
All men remaining in Britain as slaves will be sterilized. A million or two of the young women of the Nordic type will be segregated in

a number of stud farms, where, with the assistance of picked German sires, they will during a period of ten or twelve years produce nearly annually a series of Nordic infants to be brought up in every way as Germans.
These infants will form the future population of Britain. They will be partially educated in Germany, and only those who fully satisfy nazi requirements will be allowed to return to Britain and take up permanent residence. The rest will be sterilized and sent to join the slave gangs in Germany. Thus in a generation or two the British will disappear.
The editor then makes this comment:
You may think that no nation would do such a thing as this-not even Germany. But remember it is actually being done in Poland to-day.
So we know what is in store for us, if Hitler wins the war.
At the end of 1940 the national debt of Germany was 79,000,000,000 reichsmarks. Germany has been spending on her war effort 5,000,000,000 reichsmarks a month, or
60.000.	000.000 reichsmarks a year. According to a dispatch in this morning's Ottawa Citizen, nazi war spending for the current year will be 6,000,000,000 reichsmarks a month, or 72,000,000,000 reichsmarks for the year, compared with an annual income rate of
100.000.	000.000 reichsmarks. Where is the money to come from? Germany is raising a very considerable part by taxation. In the year 1939 she raised by taxation 23,600,000,000 reichsmarks. During the present fiscal year ending 31 March, 1941, she expects to raise by taxation 30,000,000,000 reichsmarks.
In Germany, tax collections take about one-third of Germany's total national income, according to Mr. G. F. Towers, governor of the Bank of Canada, in his annual report to the finance minister tabled on February 11, 1941. He makes this statement:
In Canada, during the same period, dominion government revenues will be about one-sixth of total national income. In the United Kingdom the proportion will probably be something more than one-fifth. Including the levies of the states (or provinces) and local governments, the German people are paying in taxes at least one-third more, in relation to their income, than are the people of Canada. In addition to formal taxes, Germans have also to make substantial direct payments to their government in the form of party dues, winter relief fund donations, and other special "contributions" which are just as compulsory as taxes.
Apart from taxation, most of Germany's financing has been done by borrowing. Up to 1935, borrowing was mainly done by the issue of short-term bills. From 1935 to 1938, financing mainly took the form of long-term loans. Since then, they have been experimenting with short-term delivery certificates

War Appropriation Bill
and " tax certificates," but since the commencement of the war, almost entirely with five-and ten-year notes.
Everyone in Germany who has money is compelled to lend it to the government whether he wishes to or not. Most of the borrowing is done from the financial institutions. The borrowings are spoken of as loans, but they are really taxes, because nazi leaders openly admit that the loans will never be repaid.
To build up her war effort Germany has, by means of controls, greatly lessened consumption. Interest rates are much higher in Germany than in Canada. In 1933, the interest rate on high-class government securities was 6 and 7 per cent. It has been reduced from time to time so that the general rate now paid by the German government is 4 per cent. The reductions were made not by agreement with the creditors, but by government decree. Germany also adds to her treasury by levying on the Jews and other unfortunate minorities, and by looting the overrun countries and selling the loot.
According to an article by Frederick T. Birchall in yesterday's New York Times, speaking of Germany's finances:
Every invaded country, whether it resisted or not, has been systematically ransacked for all that was valuable in it. Its stores of gold, its currency reserves, its arms and military equipment, the rolling stock of its railroads and a large part of its industrial plant have been removed to Germany.
Working for reich
By the hundreds of thousands, labourers and skilled workers have been sent to the reich to do Germany's work and leave her man power free for military service. Hundreds of thousands more are working for Germany, producing military equipment and supplies, in their home factories. Unless they work for Germany they and their families cannot eat. It has been estimated that already nazism has enlisted 2,500,000 conscript labourers in the conquered countries, that they have contributed $1,275,000,000 to German national resources and are producing probably $400,000,000 worth of supplies annually for the war.
Every occupied country pays an amount far in excess of actual cost for the maintenance of the German armies of occupation that hold it in subjection. The French are assessed
144,000,000,000 francs (about $2,800,000,000) annually for the German occupation. Norway pays $1,870,000,000, more than a third of her national income, to her military jailers. She is being bled white, but so are the other countries From the resources of all combined, Germany is paying a large part of the cost of her war. The nazis even make a source of profit. Fines are laid upon communities which show a tendency to resist domination. Only last week disorders in Amsterdam were punished hy infliction of a fine of $8,000,000 against the city.
Of all the conquered countries Poland is admittedly in the most wretched plight. A million Poles have died in concentration camps
and prisons and of starvation and exposure outside them. Thousands have been deported to hard labour in Germany. Mass arrests and deportations take place constantly without apparent cause. Labour is compulsory for all, under pain of being sent to concentration camps, and all Poles without exception must surrender thirty per cent of their meagre wages under pretext of contributing to the "reconstruction of Poland".
Germany has also been forcing the smaller nations to deliver goods to her and is paying for them in reichsmarks. Germany issued Rm. 10,000,000,000 of "printed money" plus billions of special credit bills and IOIJs to finance in conquered countries. These reichsmarks and IOUs are offered for sale in the stock markets of the world, but they are almost worthless. A person cannot legally buy reichsmarks abroad and take them into Germany and use them there. These are the only novel financial methods carried out in Germany.

One hundred ships now would certainly be much better than five hundred or a thousand when the war is over. Ships are as important as food and guns. We all realize this. Under the terms of the United States lease-lend bill which has just been passed, this principle has been recognized. The hon. member who spoke a few minutes ago mentioned Lord Beaver-brook's appeal. Lord Beaverbrook stressed this in a broadcast to the empire a few days ago. He said that we in Canada should procure ships wherever they can be obtained.
What policy the government has in this matter I do not know, but I presume every effort is being made by them at the present time to procure ships. Where these ships can be built is the problem of the Minister of Munitions and Supply. It is also the great concern of the Canadian people and the people of the British empire. The minister has told us on different occasions that with regard to production he is interested only in results and proposes to obtain supplies where they can be obtained most readily. I have no quarrel with that statement of the minister. But in carrying it out I would ask that he make no mistakes and that he use his very best judgment as to where these supplies should be obtained.
We in the maritime provinces feel that the minister and his department have more or less overlooked us. I contend that more ships should be built in the maritime provinces and particularly in my own province of New Brunswick. I have not heard the minister say whether wooden ships are suitable for use. I have seen comment in the press and heard statements that wooden ships would be useful and should be produced. If that is the fact, I point out to the minister that the maritime provinces are the logical place in which to build wooden ships as well as steel ships. It is not necessary for me to
[ Mr. Brooks.]
say here that at one time the maritime provinces were the largest producers of ships in the world. I am told that some years ago 57 per cent of the ships of British registry sailing out of Liverpool had been built on the bay of Fundy between Nova Scotia and New Brunswick. I also remember that during the last war many ships were built on the bay of Fundy and other sections of the maritimes. We have a tradition and background of shipbuilding; we are a maritime people, and if any industry is suitable for the maritime provinces, surely the shipbuilding industry is the outstanding one.
The minister spoke about building ships in the city of Saint John. I know they have been built there and that, as the minister stated, they are trying to extend their facilities in order to do more.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Trying to get some men.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Well, there are lots of
men in the maritime provinces, and I am not satisfied that the minister's statement that men cannot be got to build ships is accurate.
Another advantage in building ships in the maritime provinces, as well as on the Pacific coast, is that we are not icebound for five or six months of the year. If a ship is built on the great lakes or the St. Lawrence early in the winter, it is held up there until the spring. A ship built in the maritime provinces or British Columbia is already on the seaboard. There are also other advantages which might be mentioned.
Then there is the matter of financial assistance, which is a sore point in the maritime provinces at the present time. I should like to call attention to the treatment we have received in New Brunswick, and I refer to page 923 of Hansard, where there is a digest of Canadian and British capital assistance to industry, including some 220 items, with a capital expenditure of some 1307,000,000. Of the 220 plants throughout Canada which have received assistance, only one is in New Brunswick. That is in the town of Campbellton, and the amount involved is less than $200,000. We have not been fairly treated, in this regard, and I think it is time that at least some consideration should be given our part of Canada. I do not think one plant in Prince Edward Island has received any assistance, although I believe it has 'been given help in other ways. In this connection I should like to refer to an article which appeared recently in the New Glasgow Evening News. This article speaks of the assistance given to industry in other parts of Canada, and says:
But by and large, the maritimes are producing nothing.

War Appropriation Bill
That, of course, is an exaggeration; but their production does not compare with that of other parts of Canada.
That in spite of the fact that Ottawa on behalf of the Canadian and British governments, has authorized the construction of far more than 100 new plants.
It is more than two hundred.
This is a tremendous development, costing many hundreds of millions of dollars. But its net result when the war is over will be only to increase the industrial disparity of the rest of Canada and the maritimes.
That is a true statement.
Yet we do our share of supporting war loans (better than other sections), Red Cross and other drives, as well as all types of recruiting.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Is my hon. friend not aware
that we have given capital assistance amounting to three and a half million dollars to New Glasgow and Trenton? What do they think is their share?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
It took
them months to get that much.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
I know that assistance has been given. We get a little hand-out once in a while; we do not deny that; but I am speaking of the broad principle. I do not think we have received our share. We have over a million people in the maritime provinces, and if we received our share in proportion to the rest of Canada it would not be three and a half million dollars but a great deal more. Then this article goes on to ask this question:
What's wrong? Is it our fault? Have we lost the ability to become industrialists?
We were industrialists years ago.
Or are we forgotten?
I sometimes think, Mr. Chairman, that we have been forgotten, sadly forgotten. Just to show the mentality of the people in the central part of Canada in this connection, I would refer to a picture which w7as shown, at a local theatre a short time ago, entitled "The. Story of Canada's Growth." That was a beautiful picture; I enjoyed seeing it; but what did we find as far as the maritime provinces were concerned? One of the highlights w7as a Dutchman driving an oxcart through the village of Lunenburg. Another scene a Scotsman trying to squeeze the last inch of soil out of a barren hillside, although we have thousands of acres of good, fertile land in the maritimes. A further scene pictured a tarpaper shack with some lumbermen emerging from it. That is the sort of advertising w7e received as far as this picture was concerned. There was only one bright spot in it, the part showing the building of ships;
that was the only instance in which the maritime provinces were shown in a good light.
What was the situation with regard to Ontario? Factory after factory was shown booming; the wheels of industry were turning to capacity. We were shown the great offices of the leading businessmen of Toronto. One man called up Edmonton and said that certain goods would be shipped by airmail. Another man wras shown telephoning his representative in Vancouver that he would look after certain matters. That is the sort of comparison which leads us to believe that we are a forgotten people. In war all sections bear their full share. I was veiy glad to see in a recent article that the Minister of National War Services has become interested in the further development of industry in Canada.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Is he taking a hand in this, too?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Evidently he is. The article to which I refer mentions the appointment of a committee of three representatives, under a policy designed not so much to decentralize future war industry that Canada may create, although this will be part of its function, but rather to distribute as widely as possible across the dominion the new industries that are expected to settle in this country as a result of the disturbances in Europe. The representative for the maritime provinces is Mr. Matheson, of Moncton. I know Mr. Matheson; I believe he is an energetic man, and no doubt if he is allowed to do so he will be of great help to the maritime provinces and eastern Canada. I think this is a sound policy; I hope it goes beyond sound, as far as the minister is concerned, and that something will be done along the line suggested. Canada cannot be a great country while the central part does all the manufacturing and the extremes, such as the maritimes, have no share in industry.
We have been told that one reason why there is not more industry in New Brunswick is that we have not the power. I know that our power in New Brunswick is limited; but since w7e are spending millions of dollars in other parts of Canada, why could not a few million be spent in order to produce more power in New Brunswick? At Grand Lake we have a large power plant, which could be expanded. We have plenty of coal, and I have been given to understand that power can be produced from coal as cheaply as from water. We are told that the development of the St. Lawrence is to be proceeded with. That also reacts against us in the maritimes. We will get no advantage from the development of the St. Lawrence, although we will
War Appropriation Bill

help pay for it. The excuse being used is that more power is required in the central provinces. The power development in the St. Lawrence river will not have been completed until the war is over. I believe the people of Canada realize that fact. Nevertheless we are asked to spend money from eastern Canada to develop more power in Ontario. In other words, more industry is taken away from us, and we must pay for it.
That policy is not fair. I pick up my Montreal paper each morning and I see in it pictures depicting the distance the icebreaker has moved up the St. Lawrence river. Perhaps I cannot criticize those pictures, because they arise through a practice which has been established over many years. But I wonder if hon. members realize that again, in connection with the operation of that icebreaker in the St. Lawrence river, we at Saint John and Halifax are helping to pay for something that is taking work away from those ports and our workmen.
We are told it is in the general interest. We have no great objection to helping anything which is in the general interest, but we do suggest that there should and must be a limit to this sort of thing. We are not looking for hand-outs or special concessions. We are seeking an opportunity of throwing our full weight into Canada's war effort.
Another point is that an equal burden in our war effort should be borne by all people. Anyone who will look over the list of recruits from one end of Canada to the other will find that we in New Brunswick have done as well as, if not better than, any other section in Canada. Our young men are still looking for a chance to enlist. Why? Because there is no industry in which they may take part. If in that province we have no industry in which they may be absorbed, if there is no outlet for young men, except on farms where we produce at a loss, we are again handicapped. However, I shall say nothing further about that now. There is only one outlet for our young men, so far as the war effort is concerned, and that is for them to enlist. Anyone who will tell me that a young man working in a factory is doing as great a service for his country as the man who takes his life in his hands is telling me something I cannot believe and I know hon. members will not believe.
This is a serious matter, and I would ask that the government give it careful consideration. We cannot keep this great Canada of ours united if one section of the country is prosperous, and another section is struggling for its very existence. What we need in Canada to-day is men of vision, men who can see beyond the narrow confines of their own provinces, men who will work for the good

and interests of the whole dominion. We want to have established in Canada a great country-not a great country in the centre, but a great country from the Atlantic to the Pacific.

I cannot allow a discussion on shipbuilding, and particularly the building of wooden ships, to pass without at least taking some small part in it, particularly in view of the fact that I come from what I believe is or should be the banner shipbuilding constituency in Canada. I think it was around 1870 or 1880 that we had in .my constituency more registered ships of the type then in use than any other place in the world.
I listened with keen interest to the observations of the minister when he explained his difficulties in connection with mechanics. I know of shipyards in my constituency

speechtext: If the hon. member who has just interrupted does not know enough geography to know where the constituency of Shelburne-Yarmouth-Clare is situated, then I suggest that his constituents should elect someone else to the riding he represents at the present time.

speechtext: Tell us about it.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY

speechtext: I know of two shipyards in my constituency which have turned down orders offered to them by the government. Someone may wonder why that has taken place. I am going to give some of those reasons, briefly, and make a suggestion as to how the condition could be remedied, to the benefit of the shipbuilding industry. One of the reasons for the turning down of offered contracts is that our shipyards have turned out smaller and less expensive ships than those mentioned in the government tenders. They have turned out schooners valued at say $10,000 or $15,000, whereas the ships mentioned in the government contracts were of a type which would be valued at $50,000, $60,000 or $85,000. That would be a type of ship, the building of which some of the shipyards in that constituency would find it difficult to finance. It was

Yes; their financial capacity was lacking. When those orders were turned down there were men in the vicinity who

could have been hired to do the work of carpenters. They had material sufficient to complete the ships; but they lacked the credit, and I suggest that is one of the factors which has brought about the condition to which the minister has referred. It appears to me that some method must be adopted which would remedy this difficulty, so far as the construction of wooden ships is concerned. speechtext: When the committee took recess at six o'clock I was discussing the difficulties being faced by some of the shipyards in my constituency. I would not want it to be thought that I am talking about all shipyards in western Nova Scotia. There are some about the financial standing of which I have not full particulars, and I have never had an opportunity to discuss this matter with those in charge. To finance a ship costing $50,000 necessitates a deposit of 10 per cent, or $5,000.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: What kind of ship can be built for $50,000?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: A mine-sweeper.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: They cost $550,000.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
I am sorry to differ with the hon. gentleman who has just interrupted me, but I know that the hulls of wooden mine-sweepers are being built for $50,000. The shipyard must put out another $10,000 or $12,000 for material and there will be labour costs of $5,000 or $10,000 before they can get a cent from the government by way of an instalment payment. If a yard is building four or five ships of that type it would need capital or credit of between $75,000 and $100,000.
In the last fifteen or twenty years wooden shipbuilding in the maritimes has suffered a slump. The result has been that many family shipyards have gone down and their credit has been used up. To-day many of these shipyards find it difficult to finance to the tune I have indicated. At the risk of repeating what I said before recess, may I say that the trained labour to do this work is available and the necessary material can be found in
the vicinity; yet orders for wooden ships are going past our door simply because in some instances credit is lacking.
Many of the shipyards are equipped to build only one or perhaps two ships at a time; they oannot build four, five or six at once. If they were given proper encouragement by the government, the tonnage could be increased a great deal. Then the government is often quite tardy in making the instalment payments under contracts which have been let.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: The government is slow pay.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
The government is good pay, but it is sometimes slow. This affects the production of tonnage to a certain extent. Many of these yards have bad to wait for their money and sometimes they hesitate to take another contract. Something could be done by way of rushing payments. Another reason for the falling off in tonnage is the long period which seems to elapse between the calling of tenders by Great Britain and the awarding of contracts. In order to bring about increased production of tonnage, some improvement might be made in this connection. If the four things to which I have referred were taken care of, I think we would have an increased production from our wooden shipyards.
Last fall I spoke about wooden shipbuilding and urged that we adopt some policy which would bring about a greater production of cargo ships. I realized at the time that there was some difficulty in connection with gross tonnage of wooden ships as well as in connection with getting the necessary speed for convoy service. I have since discussed the matter with sea captains, shipbuilders, designers and the like, and I have come to the conclusion that what we should do in Canada is to build what was known in the last war as composite ships. In the last war, as at the present time, Canada built both steel and wooden ships, but we did not build any of the composite type.
During the last war the United States built ships of this type with tonnages of from
3,000	to 4,000 tons. The beams, frame and ribs were of steel, the rest of the ship being of wood. I have in my hand' a blueprint of a ship of 3,500 tons. Its length is 269 feet, its breadth 45 feet and its depth 24 feet. These ships could be built with a speed sufficient to take part in convoys, and they would take care of the shortage of tonnage which we seem to be approaching quite rapidly.
Many of our shipyards could build these ships. We have the wood necessary to build them and they could be built to last for from fifteen to twenty years, long enough to
War Appropriation Bill

get through the struggle now facing us. We have the wooden shipbuilding mechanics available to do the work and it would not be necessary to train new men. By building this type of ship, considerable steel would be saved. In the last war I think we built between 150,000 and 200,000 tons a year of wooden ships. If we in Canada were to make an effort to construct wooden and composite ships, we could reach the same tonnage. If we consider that in Great Britain, for example, the output is only about a million tons a year, in the United States between two and three million tons a year, and that the world tonnage is but little more than twenty millions, an additional production in Canada of two or three hundred thousand tons would be of great importance and value in these days of short tonnage and of the urgency of supplying transportation in convoys. While perhaps this is in some degree a new venture so far as Canada is concerned, it must not be forgotten that in the last war we built wooden ships, steel ships and even, I believe, cement ships. I have discussed this matter in my own constituency with captains who served on these composite ships in the last war. They told me they were fine vessels, having a speed of twelve or thirteen knots; one captain had a ship of 3,200 tons, and I gathered, in our discussion, that the boat was well suited to convoy work.
I suggest, therefore, that the minister and the government consider seriously the advisability of developing a programme of building composite ships. If those parts which are composed of steel or iron could be fabricated according to a standard in some of our steel plants, probably they might be sent to different yards and the boats constructed by the builders of our wooden ships. That, in my opinion, is the proper and the best way to utilize the wooden shipyards for cargo tonnage ships, and it is a thought which I desire to emphasize at this time.
In conclusion, it seems to me that we should arrange to provide credits for the development of the wooden shipyards, through the provision of both working capital and additional equipment and machinery. If, by using the materials and the men available, we can produce a wooden ship which will operate efficiently under convoy conditions, I believe we shall have done all we can as Canadians in wooden ships in this struggle for ships, ships, and yet more ships.
