subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
I desire
to say only a few words before the conclusion of this debate on the war appropriation bill. From all parts of the chamber has come a great deal and a great variety of discussion. Of course, we of this group realize how tremendous is the appropriation which we are invited to vote under this bill, and we well understand that ministers have a great deal of work to do in connection with the war programme. It is a tremendous job, but this is also a tremendous war, so I think every hon. member should be entitled to criticize the government constructively in order that the greatest amount of effort shall be put behind the prosecution of the war.
I have just been reading a reported statement by Mr. Bullitt, former United States ambassador to France, to the effect that no country can really get down to business in the matter of war preparations until a few bombs have been dropped on them, and I have often thought that it might stimulate our war production if a few bombs were dropped here in Canada; we would then begin to realize that a real war is going on. I am convinced that we are not exerting our maximum effort. I do not say that the government is not doing its best, but that best is not good enough under present conditions.
Criticism of the government by hon. members, no matter where they sit, should be regarded as intended, not to hinder but rather to stimulate the government's war effort. The government takes decidedly the wrong attitude, therefore, when ministers become peeved at the criticism which is offered from the opposite side of the chamber. Some of them seem to have almost reached the point of mental break-down; they become slightly hysterical, and certainly irritable, at some of the criticisms. This attitude was evident the other day in ministerial references to the press. I have not found, in any criticism which I have read in the newspapers, any evidence of a desire to interfere with or hinder our war effort. To my mind it is the duty and the right of the press to criticize any government when it believes that that government needs criticism. I am quite aware of the attitude which ministers have taken towards some of their critics, but I assert that it is the duty, the privilege and the right of everyone in a democratic country to criticize when in his opinion the occasion calls for it. I believe everybody is most desirous of assisting this government in every way possible. That is certainly true of some of the provincial governments. Alberta has probably received the greatest amount of criticism and

War Appropriation Bill
has suffered more than any other province from discrimination, especially at the hands of the present dominion government. Yet here is what Alberta, through its legislature, said the other day:
War savings drive given endorsation in Alberta house.
In the face of solid opposition by independent members, a resolution endorsing the federal government's war savings campaign and urging upon the federal government "the necessity of adopting effective methods of financing the war and preparing for the post-war period by the national control and issue of money without inflation" was passed in the Alberta legislature to-day.
The resolution also urged that "every citizen of Alberta should cooperate with the dominion government in the winning of the war in every reasonable w7ay possible."
The division was 35-18.
What did the provincial government ask the people of the legislature and the province of Alberta to do? First, to endorse the federal government's war savings campaign. Surely this dominion government is agreeable to that. Yet the opposition in the legislature of Alberta, instead of showing the same spirit of cooperation that the Social Credit members of parliament in this house have displayed towards the federal government, divided on that issue and voted solidly against endorsing the dominion government's war savings campaign. The vote on the resolution was 35 to 18, and the minority consisted of independents. Who are the . independents in Alberta? They are made up of Liberals and Conservatives, and so far as I know, the only thing they are independent of is the people.
The second point was the necessity of adopting effective methods of financing the war. Who in the world could honestly and sincerely oppose the federal government's adopting effective methods of financing the war? I cannot understand any sane, intelligent people voting against such a thing.
The third was the issue of money without inflation. Surely those Liberals and Conservatives in Alberta do not advocate inflation; yet that is what they did when they voted against that.
The resolution further urged that:
Every citizen of Alberta should cooperate with the dominion government in the winning of the war in every reasonable way possible.
Can you understand, Mr. Chairman, any people voting against that? Yet Liberals and Conservatives in Alberta, did so. That may be their idea of cooperation, but I am sure this federal government would not appreciate cooperation like that from the opposition in this chamber. There was a division of thirty-five to eighteen in the Alberta legislature. May I point out that no other organization in 14873-88
all the dominion has given this federal government the support that the province of Alberta has given, in every way possible, as far as this war is concerned. The only thing they are concerned about, the only thing we are concerned about in our criticism of this government, is that we should be doing more, not less, and our suggestions have always led to that.
This government, however, whether intentionally or not I do not know, seem to be critical of any criticism that may be offered; and, as I pointed out a moment ago, they took exceptional objection to the criticisms offered by the press. The Minister of Munitions and Supply (Mr. Howe) even said, referring to one newspaper, that it was the No. 1 saboteur. That is a very strong statement, and if it is true, then I think the minister should do something about it. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) the other day had this to say with reference to the press, as reported at page 1321 of Hansard:
My criticism of the press, more particularly a certain section of the press, would be this, that there is no organized group in the dominion that has done more since the fall of 1939 to delay the war effort of this country than certain sections of the press in Canada. That effort started even before war was declared, and it has been carried on since.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Who said that?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
The Minister of Agriculture and Minister of National War Services. He said that they had done more to interfere with the war effort. That must be subversive, certainly against the defence of Canada regulations. If that is true, the Minister of Agriculture should do something about it. Let us see what the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) said. At page 1231 of Hansard he is reported as saying:
As a member of parliament, I feel that the rights of parliament are supreme over the press or any other institution in the country; and if I find the press of the country misrepresenting the position as it affects the government or its war effort, I intend to take exception most emphatically to what the press says. The press is one power in the country, but I hope the day will never come when the press supplants the place that parliament is supposed to have in upholding the rights of the people. There is one other power that is supreme over press and parliament alike, namely, the people of the country; and the people of this country, on more than one occasion, have shown what they feel with respect to a press that represents a point of view contrary to that which they themselves entertain.
These are strong terms, but he goes further. Mind you, I am not saying that the Minister of Agriculture was not right, nor am I implying that the Prime Minister is not right;

War Appropriation Bill

but what I want to know is, what they will do about the matter. The Prime Minister went on to say, as reported on page 1232 of Hansard-.
I ask hon. members if that is fair criticism. Are not all these not only false insinuations but false statements? Are they not malicious statements? I go so far as to say that that article is libellous; first, because it is false, and, second, because it is malicious, and it bears the stigma of both these things on its face. I go further and say it infringes the privileges of this house.
One minister says the press is the No. 1 saboteur; another minister says it has done more to interfere with our war effort than anything else in Canada; the Prime Minister says that these statements are malicious, libellous and false, and infringe upon the rights of the members. What is the Prime Minister going to do about it? Let us go back and see -in the statement I first read to the committee. He said: "I intend to take exception most emphatically to what the press says." Take exception! They do not care whether he takes exception to it or not.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Why should they?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Why should they? He is going to take exception to it. I could not help thinking, from the way in which the Prime Minister guarded his remarks, that the insinuation all the way through, as I understood the speech, was a direct threat to the press. Yet he adds that he will take exception to it.
I am not saying that the Prime Minister is not right, but I wish to compare the attitude of this government to criticism from the press with the attitude which they took towards the Alberta government when it had something to say about the press. The Alberta government never at any time refused the right of criticism to the press. It never called them saboteurs. It may have said that they misrepresented the facts, but this is what it had to say with regard to the act to ensure publication of accurate news and information:
Why pass:
First, because the control of news and the control of credit are both exercised by the financial interests.
Second, because "the freedom of the press" has become licence to distort news-*
I do not think the Minister of Munitions and Supply would contradict that statement. -misrepresent facts-
I think he agrees with that.
-and withhold essential information from the public.

I said, "essential information"; that is, truthful information. I think the Minister of Munitions and Supply agrees with that.
Third, because this anti-social aspect of the press, under inspired direction, is being used to thwart the people of Alberta in their struggle against finance.
What happened? Assent was withheld by the lieutenant-governor, a Liberal appointee of this government. The measure was declared unconstitutional by the Supreme Court of Canada, and on an appeal by the province of Alberta from the decision of the Supreme Court of Canada, the privy council refused to hear Alberta's argument by counsel.
What it would have done:
First, it would have ensured that all newspapers in Alberta would publish all the facts in their news reports of governmental matters, so far as this was possible-
No restriction whatever.
-and if, from any cause, false statements appeared, equal space would be given for authoritative correction.
Is that unreasonable? Had that passed, had that practice been carried on throughout Canada, I wonder if this Liberal government would have appreciated it right now.
Second, would have ensured that the same information that every publisher demands from correspondents to his columns, that is, the names of contributors of articles, would be available to the people when demanded by their representatives.
This, briefly, is all the Press Act meant. It was widely misrepresented by the press as a muzzling act; actually it was the reverse. It did not prohibit the press publishing anything it wanted; it merely provided that the public be told all the facts, not merely what a particular newspaper saw fit to publish. I wonder whether the Minister of Munitions and Supply agrees with that. I wonder whether the Prime Minister agrees with that. Yet the opposition to the Social Credit government were the very ones who opposed that Press Act. The federal government is now complaining most bitterly when the press criticize it. I think the press should have every possible privilege of criticism; but they should not be allowed to publish misrepresentations and false statements, and if they should do it under any circumstances, by intention or otherwise, then the correction should be made and given the same publicity.
The Prime Minister overlooks one fact-if he does not know it now he soon will-that the press in this country under organized finance is much stronger and more powerful than he is.

That is a privilege of members of parliament, and I do not see how the government can expect the people of Canada to have confidence in it when the members of this house have no confidence in it. I am not saying that in an unduly critical spirit, because there is no one in this country more anxious than I am to see this war carried on successfully. Never have I done anything that I know of to hinder this war effort.
I have, however, been greatly concerned by reason of our lack of effort. Why? Maybe it is because I do not know all the facts, but I certainly have been trying to find them out. I look at the newspapers and see great headlines about the quantity of munitions pouring off the line. I see pictures of a fleet of aeroplanes, giving the impression that we are putting out aeroplanes faster than the British can use them. One goes to a movie and sees, as we were shown in Ottawa the other day, a row of tanks and these aeroplanes going round. That is propaganda, and probably rightly so, to indicate what we are doing, but the impression is being given that we are doing everything that is humanly possible. I do not think that is true. It may be good propaganda, and I do not think that should be neglected, but it is definitely wrong to lull our people into false security, because it will work against us in the long run.
We are told on the radio time and time again that this is an all-out war effort. If it is I say, let us go at it; let us do it in that way. But I very much doubt that. I had an illustration which shows why I have not the confidence in the government that possibly I should have. On one occasion I went into a manufacturing plant in eastern Canada and the management told me they were then working on contracts which the government had not signed. I asked, "How do you know the government are going to accept your tender?" He said, "We do not know, but we cannot wait on this government." When a manufacturer tells you that-

I do not have to tell the hon. member, because he probably would find it if it was. One cannot expect people to have confidence in the 14873-88J
government when they find such things as that. The other day I saw in a newspaper this statement by Mr. Macaulay when he was speaking at a banquet in Toronto, I think it was on February 28 last, with the premier of Ontario:
When I know that not ten miles from here there is a great aircraft plant working at only twenty per cent capacity and know at the same time it is touch-and-go if Britain will have enough aircraft, I then wonder if Canada has wakened up.
Mr. Macaulay is a responsible member of the Ontario legislature. I do not think any citizen in his position would make a statement like that if there were not some truth in it. No matter what the government say, I cannot bring myself to believe that, when such conditions exist, we are putting forth an allout war effort.
I have travelled over western Canada a good deal and .have visited many plants in Calgaryq Edmonton, Lethbridge and Macleod, and these establishments which were manufacturing war materials in the last war are not doing anything now. I ask myself, if we are having an all-out war effort, why are not these plants doing something?
The other day the minister stated that we are something like three months behind expectations. That, I think, shows that the minister is not satisfied. He may be doing all he possibly can, but it leads me to believe that there is something wrong somewhere. It is up to the government to find out what and where it is. It certainly cannot be said that the people are not anxious to do everything that can be done, because everywhere I go I find that one of the most talked-of questions. Men say, "Why cannot I get a job?" I heard the minister talking about experts to-day, saying they cannot get sufficient skilled labour. Only yesterday I got a letter from a man, and I know this personally because in the early part of last winter I myself told him to write to the government. He is a trained blacksmith with years of experience, an expert electric welder and an expert acetylene welder, but he cannot get a job. When I was going home on the train last year I met a man coming from Quebec, a young French fellow, who told me he had spent seven years working on a lathe. He could not get a job; he was going out to British Columbia to see if he could get work with a private concern. He told me that he had waited for three weeks in Montreal trying to get a job with a firm having a government contract, but he could not get employment with them. Nevertheless the government say now they cannot get experienced workmen. When I see the conditions that exist I can hardly bring myself to believe that statement.

The other day I received a resolution passed by the city council of Drumheller and signed by Mr. Harold A. Brown, city clerk and treasurer. These people are greatly concerned about our war effort. Sometimes I think it would do the members of the government good if they would just travel around among the people and find out what they are thinking. After all, it is the people who must be behind our war effort, and if we have not their confidence we cannot get very far. This is what the city of Drumheller has to say:
The mayor and members of the council of the city of Drumheller hereby go on record of their support of the efforts which have been made to date by the Drumheller board of trade, the Drumheller junior chamber of commerce and other organizations in this community to obtain location at Drumheller of some of these wartime enterprises.	,
And further go on record in their submission that the city of Drumheller and district is not receiving fair and reasonable consideration in this regard and request the government of the Dominion of Canada and its proper ministers and officers to take under consideration the claims of this city and district to have established here one or more of the schemes created for the furtherance of Canada's war effort.
And that the field army workshop No. 0 R.C.O.C.R.A. be established as a permanent force with headquarters at the said city.
This council hereby undertaking on behalf of itself as a corporate body, its members and the citizens of Drumheller and district as a whole to continue their whole-hearted support of the government of this dominion in the prosecution of the war and in particular undertaking to cooperate and assist our dominion and the various departments thereof with reference to making available the facilities of this community in connection with the establishment of any war-time undertaking here.
In view of that, no one can tell me that the people of Drumheller are not greatly concerned; and as they see the hundreds of unemployed, they ask themselves the very same question I am asking: what is the matter? Is this an all-out war effort? We go around and see plants idle; we see aircraft factories not working to capacity. What is the matter? Surely something must be wrong. The other day the Minister of Munitions and Supply suggested that hon. members should visit these factories, and I think he was quite right. He should, however, make it possible and convenient for members to visit these munition plants, gun and aircraft factories, military centres, barracks and air-training centres. It is the duty of hon. members to make these visits, but I believe the government should issue blanket passes to all members of parliament to enable them to gain admission to these places. Hon. members should visit these Bren gun and aircraft factories; they should talk to the management and see what is going on, in order to know whether or not everything possible is being done.

As a matter of fact, I think it will work in the opposite way. I believe it would be decidedly wrong for the government to carry on this census under these conditions.
I should like for a few minutes to refer to the salvage scheme. I do not think any section of Canada has contributed more to

our war effort than have the prairie provinces. When one considers what the farmers have contributed, are contributing and are expected to contribute, with absolutely no profit but rather a loss to themselves, no hon. member can say that western Canada is not doing its share and possibly more than its share. Now we are asked to support a salvage campaign. I have no objection to that; if it is necessary, it should be done, but one thing about it surprises me. In a letter we received some time ago from the Minister of National War Services we were urged to collect scrapiron. and were told that it was one of the most essential things at the present time. Perhaps he is right, but on February 26 we received a letter signed by Mr. Justice T. C. Davis, associate deputy minister of the Department of National War Services, in which we find this statement with regard to scrapiron:
Scrap cannot be economically moved at_ the moment from Saskatchewan, Alberta or British Columbia owing to the fact the point of consumption is largely in the Hamilton area, in Ontario, and the freight rate on these commodities from these provinces to this point is such that it is practically impossible to economically move this material.
At the moment negotiations are under way with the railway companies to try to get them to reduce the freight rates on material of this kind, gathered in these provinces by voluntary organizations, created according to the terms of my letter of February 5. We are also in consultation with the steel controller and expect to be in consultation with the steel companies to see if we cannot get an increase in the price of scrap gathered in these provinces by organizations created in accordance with the terms of the said letter.
This is the thing which, if it were not so serious, would be funny. The government pleads for scrap iron. Then Mr. Justice Davis tells us that scrap iron cannot be economically moved from Saskatchewan, Alberta and British Columbia. If that movement is essential to our war services, why bicker with the railway companies to see whether or not we can get reduced freight rates? Why not tell them what you want to do? That is what you are doing to the labourer; that is what you are doing to the farmer. Why not tell the railway companies what you want to do, and not deal with them as the Minister of Transport tried to deal with me a short time ago in connection with the matter of elevators in western Canada, when he placed the blame on the board of railway commissioners.
The course taken by the government is not a serious war effort. Let us get down to realities. Let us merit the confidence of the people. Not by such acts as I have mentioned will the government merit it. It is stated that movement cannot be made economically because the only place where the scrap iron
can be used is in Hamilton. Some time ago a request was made that the government open the rolling mills in Calgary. Those mills operated at the time of the last war, and the machinery used at that time is there to-day.

speechtext:
I promise the minister I shall be exceedingly brief. I wish to deal with two topics, both of which are germane to the resolution before the committee. One arises directly from this evening's debate with respect to shipbuilding.
I shall ease the minister's mind at once by telling him that I am not in a critical mood this evening. Rather would I hope with regard to this Darticulax matter to make some con-
War Appropriation Bill

structive suggestions. I heard with a great deal of interest, and subsequently read with equal interest the progress report made by the Minister of National Defence for Naval Services (Mr. Macdonald) last November at the opening of the session. I was particularly interested in that part of his speech which dealt with naval construction in Canada, when he told us that the government had been making certain types of naval vessels, such as corvettes and mine-sweepers, and in which he visualized the building of destroyers and cruisers in Canada.
I recall that when the Minister of Munitions and Supply (Mr. Howe) returned from England he made an announcement, first, I believe in the United States before he reached Canada, and subsequently amplified in Canada, that tlie Canadian government for the account of the British government would undertake the construction of a substantial number of freighters, due, of course, to the losses in British tonnage which had been sustained through submarine warfare. All of this was heartening. But when one comes to analyse the statements which have been made, he will see at once, and become convinced that all these are directly attributable to the war effort, and to the war effort alone.
Not for one minute do I condemn that. It is absolutely as it should be, and in so far as the government has gone I desire to commend it. Just how far it has gone in the construction of various types, the minister will perhaps inform the house at a later time.
In this connection I am reminded that last evening over the radio we had the pleasure of listening to a speech by the president of Vickers in Montreal, in which he dilated for fifteen minutes-I assume under the auspices of the bureau of information

upon the programme of construction of war vessels and freighters-all of which was heartening. I would suggest to the ministry to-night that it take a little longer view of this question of shipbuilding. We have heard a good deal to-day about loss of industry in the maritime provinces. May I point out to the committee and the country that if there is any part of Canada constituted favourably for the development of steel shipbuilding, it is the maritime provinces, where we find the conjunction of coal and steel. I am not as old as some hon. members, and perhaps a good deal older than others, but I recall the days when the Dominion Iron and Steel company was first established on the island of Cape Breton. That huge plant was established at that point because the relationship of the natural resources of Cape Breton to the iron mines in Newfoundland stood in a particularly happy position, so far as the export trade of Canada was concerned.

I believe Mr. Fielding was Minister of Finance at that time, and I remember how he endeavoured by a policy of bonusing to establish the steel industry in Nova Scotia. That industry has had its ups and downs, fortunes and misfortunes; but to-day I believe, if we view it in the light of what it is doing in connection with the war effort and for the British government, it must be recognized at once that no matter what may have been the cost to the country in days gone by, it is a good thing for Canada and for Great Britain that to-day that huge industry operates in the bluenose province of Nova Scotia.
May I impress this point upon the ministry: The maritime provinces have suffered industrially and geographically. I have never disguised from myself the fact that geography has been against New Brunswick and Nova Scotia from the point of view of interprovincial trade. If I needed any reminder of that fact, all I would have to do would be to read the report my hon. friend the Minister of National Defence for Naval Services published some years ago when he first became premier of Nova Scotia, and when I thought they overplayed their hand a little bit too much.
I do not want to make anything like a political speech to-night and I shall come immediately to the point. We have in this government some important men; there are a number of key men, members who are endeavouring to do their duty to the countiy and to the nation. They are doing their duty as they see it in connection with the war effort. I often think, however, that this is not the only duty that devolves upon them as occupants of the treasury benches.
From time to time we have been reminded in this house that there will be a post-war situation in Canada. Unless we take time by the forelock and endeavour to develop some new ideas, that period is going to be a sad time for this dominion. I should like to make a constructive suggestion to the com-mitee and to the country. I should like to impress upon the ministry, especially those members who are from the maritime provinces, that they begin now to visualize a future for the maritime provinces by the recapturing of our industrial position. I can see no greater scope for the effort of the government than in connection with steel shipbuilding.
During the past summer I had the honour to address the Commercial club of Halifax, and I outlined at considerable length to the merchants, manufacturers and business men of Halifax there assembled the opportunity which would come once more to the maritime provinces by recapturing and rebuilding

War Appropriation Bill
the position which had been lost, largely through our own inertia. I put to them this alternative: Shall the business men of the maritime provinces seek to take advantage of the opportunity which will present itself presently to rebuild the industrial status of our provinces, or shall they continue just to sit down and draw their bank and other dividends, as they have done in days gone by, rather than exert themselves to build up for the future?
I am optimist enough to believe that there is an opportunity in Nova Scotia and New Brunswick to build up a steel shipbuilding industry that will carry us on to new adventure and new profits in the post-war period. We have heard, in days gone by, that in times of peace we cannot compete with England in the building of steel tonnage because our costs are too high and perhaps we have not the skilled labour. These offer a challenge to our people. In days gone by, the government has spent substantial sums of money upon dry docks and shipbuilding plants in the maritime provinces. These dry-docks and plants are now occupied to capacity, but largely on repair work.
As soon as I read that the Minister of Munitions and Supply had returned to Canada with a programme for the construction of 9,000-ton freighters, I thought immediately of the possibilities with respect to the plant at Saint John. I was told that without a substantial capital expenditure it would not be possible to lay keels for 9,000-ton ships. But if given the opportunity, which I believe they will be given, they could lay keels for 6,000-ton, 5.000-ton and 4,000-ton ships which would be of great advantage to Great Britain at the present time, as well as in the post-war period. There are enough men with enterprise and ambition to take up this matter, and there is still capital in the maritime provinces.
I suggest to my hon. friends from the maritime provinces who are in the ministry that, no matter how engulfed they are with their war work-and I know they are so engulfed- they get together and bring into consultation the best brains available with marine knowledge to see if a plan cannot be mapped out for the establishment of a steel shipbuilding industry in the provinces of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick. If they do that, a generation down there will rise up and call them blessed. I have lived a good many years in that section of Canada and I have seen one old family company after another fold up and pass out of the picture. This has been one of the most distressing experiences in my whole life.
Fifty years ago, those provinces were teeming with small industries. I think we made a great mistake in Canada when we failed to support the maintenance of small industrial units. We have been so imbued and impressed with the example of our friends in the United States; we have felt that everything must be done on a huge scale, that there must be great mass production, and we have lost sight of what to me is a most important factor to the community and to the nation. We should maintain as far as is economically possible small industrial units throughout the country. I throw out this suggestion to the ministers in the utmost good faith and ask them to give it consideration.
There is a large dry dock at Saint John and another at Halifax, both built with government subventions. These dry docks do intermittent work during peace time, but a programme of steel shipbuilding would give them the necessary backlog to retain their artisans and skilled workers. They are not as scarce as the Minister of Munitions and Supply thinks they are. I was told that -the Saint John company had stepped up its personnel from 400 to 1,200, and they may take on still more. It may be necessary to train some men. I believe that the genius of our people and their desire to see a rehabilitation of this industry in the maritime provinces is sufficient to overcome what are insuperable difficulties in the minds of some persons, but which fade into insignificance when one gets down to realities. I feel sure that once more the people of the maritimes, with the vision they have had in days gone by, will be able to come forward and regain, in part at least, the position which they occupied in older days.
What part of Canada is more favourably situated for export trade than the maritime provinces? Why have we not the export trade we ought to have. I know it is the custom to blame everything upon central Canada, but that is not the whole story. Part of the story is the fact that after the civil war in the United States, after the good times that came then to our seaports, our exporters were content to consolidate their gains, to sit down and invest their money in bank stocks and things like that; in other words, to rest upon their oars. The maritime provinces should have seized their opportunity and built up a sound industry of steel shipbuilding. Where would we be to-day? Therefor I say to the members of the government, those who are charged with the responsibility to-day:	Do not be so engulfed in your
duties in connection with the operation of the war, important though they are; have a little vision and let all of us get together,
War Appropriation Bill

perhaps round a table, and see if we cannot do something to further that which is so dear to my heart, at all events.
There is just one other observation I wish to make. In the very much abbreviated statement, covering as it does less than four pages of Hansard, which the Minister of Finance (Mr. Usley) made on February 18 when he introduced this resolution, he, having announced this huge expenditure, omitted- and I am not saying this in a critical sense- to tell the people of Canada and this house how he proposed to get this money. Before this resolution is reported out of the committee, I invite him to do so. How much of this money is to be raised by taxation? I do not suggest for a moment that he should tell us what, if any, new taxes should be imposed; that, of course, would neither be proper for me to ask nor for him to disclose. But what I should like to know is, just how much of this $1,300,000,000, or if it is now to be $1,460,000,000, are the Canadian people to be asked to pay in taxation, and how much are we to be asked to lend? I think that is a reasonable request, and if the government has arrived at a conclusion we should be told.

We are in this war, and this resolution will be passed. It will be passed in this chamber unanimously,

I imagine. At all events it will have behind it the unanimous support of our party in this house; it will have behind it unanimously the government's supporters, and I hope it will have the unanimous support of my hon. friends in the far corner, although I, cannot speak for them. Our Canadian people are thoroughly behind a maximum war effort, but we want to know. We want to know everything which can be told to us, save and except those things which might bring aid and comfort to the enemy or which might be detrimental to the war effort; and to assert that a statement that so much is to be raised by taxation, so much by loan, would be detrimental to the government's war effort is, I submit, an absolute non sequitur. We should be told in advance of the budget.
The government is now making preparation for the next loan. It will take the united effort of every class of political opinion in Canada to put this loan over. I am not unmindful and I am sure the minister is not unmindful of the last loan. That condition must not happen again. And there must be no forced loans in Canada. That would not be creditable to the Canadian people, and I am sure it will not be necessary. But in order to achieve the maximum in connection with loans, I suggest to the minister that he will have to get the united and undivided support of every class and every species of public opinion in Canada.
I tell him this, just one final word before I sit down, that he cannot get that if the government is to continue to be carried on in a partisan manner.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
I am very glad that my hon. friend took the floor before I did, because what I have to say might have rather spoiled his eloquent address.
In considering the remarks of the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Green) and the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth-Clare (Mr. Pottier) it occurred to me that I could have gone somewhat further than I did in saying the government of Canada has approved a Canadian programme of shipbuilding. I often think it is not wise to go too far into the details of that sort of thing until one is able to say just exactly what he can do and how fast he can do it. I have been criticized for making an announcement and having a time lag before we carried it out. But we are examining the situation closely to see how far that programme can succeed. We are hopeful that we can get out some additional capacity, but I am perfectly certain that it must be done in an orderly' way. We had an example in the last war of a government rushing in, late in the third year of war, with a shipbuilding

War Appropriation Bill
programme which was put out helter-skelter; almost any sort of plant which would undertake a job or accept government assistance took a contract. The result was that they got some very badly and uneconomically built boats, and they had a post-war problem which lasted for the next twenty years. We hope to be able to build in an orderly way a Canadian fleet of boats, and, of course, we shall distribute that work as widely as circumstances will permit.
My hon. friend the leader of the opposition has spoken for shipbuilding in the maritime provinces. I agree with him that from its history and its geography that section of Canada should be an ideal place to carry on a shipbuilding programme. We must nevertheless face the situation as we find it. At the time that the first corvette programme was placed, we ordered three corvettes from the St. John shipbuilding company. Those corvettes are not built yet, although other yards have turned out many times the number. I am not criticizing the St. John yard, because it has been using every man it could employ, and has searched Canada for men. I know that the company has searched the prairies and every other part of Canada in an attempt to bring shipbuilders to St. John. The fact remains that they have not been able to man their yards sufficiently to work twenty-four hours a day on the repair of ships. We refrained at that time from placing orders for new ships in Halifax, for the reason that we knew the capacity of that yard would be taxed to the limit on the overhaul of ships, and we wished all the manpower that could be collected there to be concentrated on that particular work.
After all, to obtain ships to be of use in this war, by far the most efficient method is to give a quick turn-around to the ships that are in service, and that is possible only if we have entirely adequate repair facilities at the turn-around port. I am sorry to say we have not been able to do that entirely. We have been bending every effort towards it. We have been trying to attract manpower to those ports. We have put in additional facilities and we are still building additional facilities in the hope of being able to bring that about. But I wish to make it clear that until we can have completely adequate repair and overhaul facilities for the turn-around of the boats now in service, it would be folly to attempt a large-scale programme of shipbuilding that would in any way cope with the situation affecting the present shipyards.
Another fact that stares us in the face is that a factor in the efficient use of ships is rapid loading, and there again we have not 14873-89
up to this time been able to organize the waterfront of Halifax on a twenty-four hour basis-again, for lack of man-power. We hope to do it. Until recently the docks closed at eleven in the evening and did not open until eight next morning, and Halifax, I believe, was working with only one shift of stevedores, who were working a long day.

speechtext:
The building of ships in Nova Scotia seems to have dominated the discussion in committee to-day. I know of nothing that will capture the imagination of the people of Nova Scotia more than this question, but I am sorry to say that in recent years it has been mostly imagination. The practical application has not been as good as it should have been. I believe, however, the time has arrived for a revival, for several reasons. The first is the great need of the country; second, the situation at tide-water on the eastern coast of the country; and, third, the fact that we have as Minister of Munitions and Supply (Mr. Howe) a gentleman who is eminently fitted for the position and who has knowledge of conditions in Nova Scotia. The Minister of Munitions and Supply bears the illustrious name of Howe, and I believe he is of the same blood as that great tribune of the people of Nova Scotia, the great Joseph Howe, who is still to-day considered Nova Scotia's greatest statesman.
The hon. gentleman has been Minister of Munitions and Supply in this government for some time; and as one who is interested in industry, having some little knowledge of industry in the country, I have been watching his performance. I have also seen what the press had to say, and while they have criticized him-and much of that criticism, I think, is light thinking and subtle and shows a lack of knowledge of the mechanics of the situation-I have yet to see a newspaper that has questioned his integrity, ability or industry.
rMr. Howe.]
For some years the minister lived in Nova Scotia, having been a teacher in our university of Dalhousie. He therefore knows the background of Nova Scotia and I believe that when we appeal to him, as we have done to-night, with the leader of the opposition (Mr. Hanson) backing us up in our desire for more shipbuilding in Nova Scotia, we can look to this minister with confidence that he will do something more in the near future.
This talk about delay in getting on with the war effort from a mechanical point of view suggests that many people do not appreciate what it takes to turn out a new product in the mechanical field. I recall that Henry Ford, a great mechanical genius, perhaps the greatest on the American continent, closed his plant for a whole year in order to change the model of his car; yet we want the minister to take on new products and overnight produce them so that they will be sent forward, without all the thought, work and planning which it takes to bring a new product into existence in the mechanical field.
The hon. member for Royal (Mr. Brooks) this afternoon painted a very blue picture of Nova Scotia, so much so that I would hate to live in a country that is as bad as he painted Nova Scotia. I think he was talking euphemistically when he said he saw Nova Scotia in pictures in Ottawa-

speechtext: I would be the last to say otherwise.

speechtext:
Strange to say, the shipbuilding activity my hon. friend spoke of was in the same town. Lunenburg in prosecuting the fisheries has been able to keep up shipbuilding as an efficient industry without

War Appropriation Bill
getting government aid. The shipyard in my town is now busy on private work and it is not looking to the government for work at the present time. Does the hon. member know that the government of Nova Scotia in the last year had the biggest surplus in its history? No business in Nova Scotia? This week-end I went to Toronto and was the guest of a man who is the head of a national industry with branches all across Canada, and he told me that Nova Scotia in the last two years has the best percentage of increase of any part of Canada. Business has increased twenty per cent in the last year. Surely that is not bad. Coming along in the train, I was talking to the conductor; the train was late, and he said, "Ah, well it is pretty hard to be on time"; between Moncton and Truro-I think it is about 120 miles-there are 27^ miles of cars either rolling or on sidings. That looks like good business in Nova Scotia.
To-day Halifax is the greatest maritime port in' America, perhaps in the world. The population has greatly increased. Halifax has the greatest war activity of any part of this country. It is the centre of the shipping of the world. It has one of the finest harbours in the world, and if I could go into detail- which I shall not on account of giving too much information about the war-I could amaze the committee regarding what is going on in Halifax.
In Nova Scotia we have concentrations of troops and extensive military camps that create a good deal of business. We have many air fields. At Sydney there are the great steel works, also steel works at Trenton, engaged in war industry, and all in all the province of Nova Scotia is receiving some benefit from this artificial war-time prosperity. There are poor spots in the province, for instance, the Annapolis valley where the apple-growing industry is a war casualty, but the government has appropriated $2,500,000 to relieve this situation. While we in Nova Scotia are an aggressive people and want things for the province, I do not like to come here and tell this committee that we are an inferior people, not able to look after ourselves and not willing to take our part as citizens of Canada.
Let me now say a word about shipbuilding. In the Sirois report one will find as good an historical record of the early days in Nova Scotia as one will find anywhere. It is splendid^ written and contains a great deal of information. They refer to our conditions in Nova Scotia years ago as the economy of
wind, wood and water. That is, we had the wood to build the ships, nature provided the wind to sail them-

speechtext:
-and the ocean was the road they travelled to every country in the world, to bring back the products of all quarters of the world, that brought prosperity and made life so pleasant in Nova Scotia. The days of the wooden ships were Nova Scotia's halcyon days. Nova Scotia ranked fourth in the world in shipping; it had more ships upon the seas per capita than any other country in the world. In those days the wooden sailing ship was the world's best method of ocean transportation, and Nova Scotian ships were the best. By its shipping Nova Scotia developed banks and allied industries; it had an economy that was almost perfect, and everyone now speaks of those days as the great days of Nova Scotia. But as the day of the wooden ship began to pass, Nova Scotia began to slip and they have blamed it on confederation ever since.
The wooden ship has survived in the fishing industry because in the smaller units wooden ships have advantages over the steel ship. The wooden ship is not a conductor of heat and cold and will be freer from ice. It is better for coastal navigation because if it runs into the shore it is not apt to be damaged so much, and it is cheaper. Therefore, in the smaller units the wooden ship has advantages over the steel ship. I am told also that it has an advantage with regard to the magnetic mine.
Some years ago we thought the fishing industry was doomed because the wooden sailing ship was beginning to be a thing of the past. But then came the diesel engine which has revived wooden ships, making the small wooden ship an economic unit, cheaper and I think for some purposes better than a steel ship. What the government is trying to build to-day in Nova Scotia are small wooden ships, most of them propelled by diesel engines; they are good; they are economical and, when the war is over, there will not be as much to scrap as with a steel ship.
We are having some difficulty about getting a full effort on wooden ships at present. Shipbuilding had gone down. The yards were more or less in a state of decay. To start building wooden ships at this time is a hazardous business. A man knows that, when the war is over, whatever he has invested is a total loss. Therefore, to put money into wooden shipbuilding to-day. with the income tax situation as it is whereby he is allowed to earn only about ten per cent a year and can only expect to go two or three years, is
War Appropriation Bill

not justified from a financial point of view. But there is provision in the income tax act whereby a man in a business of this kind can get a special depreciation allowance, and that might be the salvation of the wooden shipbuilders.
Some of the men who are in this business are short of capital. There are many good artisans in Nova Scotia who have men who can build ships, but they are short of funds. When we see the hundreds of millions of dollars that have been lent to industries in upper Canada, surely these builders of small wooden ships might very well be helped over the hurdle. They are going to produce a ship for you; their security is good. That situation does not prevail in my own county, but I know that it does prevail in other parts of Nova Scotia.
We should do some missionary work in this connection. These men are frightened by the specifications. The departmental officers have naval specifications obtained from England, where in days of peace they brought teak-wood from the east, and there are other points that do not apply to this country at all. These officers go to a builder in Nova Scotia, a man who is not experienced in business but who is a good ship carpenter. They say to him, "You must have this ship finished in a certain time." Well, he gets scared at once. Then they come along with a great long specification, made out for the purpose of protecting officials, and they say the ship must be built to that specification.
I know that at the present time ships are being held up because they demand keels of oak larger than we grow in the maritime provinces. A birch keel is just as good under present circumstances. The shipbuilders tell them that, but the officials do not like to change. Then they demand teak-wood in the superstructure. Teak is a very expensive wood, while the spruce we have in Nova Scotia is tough and just as good for their purpose under present conditions. I do not know why they quibble over these details instead of going ahead man fashion with the building of these wooden ships; it is hard to understand. It simply means that officialdom is protecting itself instead of going ahead and doing those things necessary in the interests of the country.

speechtext: They even want copper rivets in the life-boats.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Canada is not marine
minded. Once we had a man who was marine minded, who had vision. They said he was extravagant, but whatever else might be said of him at least he had vision. I refer to Sir Henry Thornton, who put Canada into

the business of carrying on ocean trade. He had a fleet of ships that carried Canada's products all over the world, to Australia, the West Indies and elsewhere. For years those ships showed a deficit. He put them on at a time when the wooden ship was passing out, and there was some criticism because it was felt that he was perhaps shoving the wooden ship out a little faster than it should go, but still it was a step forward. It was progress in ocean-going traffic, and for years these ships carried on until finally they got out of the red and showed a profit. Then we had a railway problem in this country. The railway was hopelessly in debt; between 1930 and 1935 we had hard times in Canada, and the government sold anything they could in order to realize some ready money. So they conceived the idea of selling these ocean going ships, the only part of the Canadian National system that anyone would buy. They sold these ships in order to realize a little money with which to make the railway situation look better.
If these ships had been retained they would have been worth a great deal to-day; as a matter of fact, they went up in value very soon after they were sold. Most of the ships were taken over by English shipping companies. When we speak of vision, what sort of progressive country is it whose efforts stop at the shore? No country ever became great without having commerce upon the sea, and Canada should have a great overseas trade. These boats did the missionary work, and do not forget that when your products go to a foreign country in your own ships you can control the freight rates. As soon as these ships were bought by the shipping ring the freights went up. No private industry in this country can compete with the shipping ring; it requires a government for that. The ring watched the situation closely, and as soon as they could do so they bought our ships. Then, when we wished to send our goods to foreign countries under such conditions that we could overcome the tariffs and other obstacles facing us, we found that one of the most necessary facilities for the transport of our goods was in other hands, and Canada's effort was circumscribed by the freight rates charged by other people.
It was a mistake to sell Canada's merchant marine. The greatness of Nova Scotia came from the sea, and Nova Scotia never will become great again except through service on the sea. Our merchant ships, although they were not built in Nova Scotia, were important to my province because Nova Scotia crews could man them; our young

War Appropriation Bill
men could become seamen, and that is the activity we desire in that province. To-day many of our young men are in the navy.
Therefore I say, in later years there has been no incentive to build ships in Nova Scotia. The government did not want ships; the minister told us that England could build ships much more cheaply than we could. I recall that concurrently with the signing of the statute of Westminster, there was passed the merchant shipping agreement, which left our coastal shipping open to practically the whole world, with no protection for our own nationals. Why, even the great United States below us, with a wealth of shipping, restricts her coastal trade to her own ships. I am not going to blame any government for disposing of these merchant ships, although I believe they were sold before this government came to power. I believe it was felt that this would bring in some easy money to help out the national economy.
I have said that this is the time for a revival. I believe we should now press forward and, even though the wooden ship is passing away, we should be building iron ships at tide-water in the province of Nova Scotia. The other day I read an editorial in the Montreal Gazette, commenting upon the fact that someone had intimated that iron ships should be built on the great lakes. There is no doubt that this would have certain advantages, principally cheap power. All the rain that falls in western Canada comes down the great lakes and through the Niagara gorge, and because of that act of God we have cheap powe. in this part of Canada. But it must be remembered that central Canada is frozen up for six months of the year, and it must be remembered also that our canal system connecting the great lakes and the St. Lawrence is extremely vulnerable in war time. If you destroy one part of it you cripple the whole structure. In Nova Scotia, while we are on the Atlantic coast, I think we are much more protected from the point of view of shipbuilding.
There is still plenty of labour in the maritime provinces. A few months ago a man came into my office seeking men to go to Montreal to build boats. There was quite a little excitement in Nova Scotia with regard to this man coaxing people to go to Montreal to build ships. I said, "If the men are not employed you cannot complain, because they should be employed. If they are employed in building ships, the order in council will not permit him to take them away, so we have not very much room for complaint." There is no reason, however, why we should
not be busy in Nova Scotia by the construction of wooden ships for a few years to come. But when this war is over, let us be building iron ships in Nova Scotia.
When I hear about spending money to help stimulate industry in other parts of Canada, I think we are justified in asking that in the maritimes we should have some stimulation and help from the government of Canada in a scientific, and perhaps in a financial way. Let us have this help to establish shipbuilding plants, so that Nova Scotia again may seek the destiny which should be hers in Canada, namely, that of a truly maritime people.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, it is after some hesitation I rise to take part in the debate. Hon. members will recall the speech delivered on December 3, by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe), following my address on the same day. In his observations the right hon. gentleman said that I was not speaking for the county of Gaspe because I had been elected by grace of a minority vote. The other day the hon. member for Pontiac (Mr. McDonald) in his turn reproached me because of circumstances which had brought about my election.
You may understand, Mr. Chairman, my hesitation. However, I took the trouble to make an incursion into that precious source of information concerning the political performances of hon. members in this august house. I refer to the Parliamentary Guide. It seemed only proper to begin my study of the results of the last general election with a survey of what happened in the constituency contested by the revered leader of this chamber, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King). This is what I find at page 319 under the heading "Prince Albert, Saskatchewan":
General election 1940:
King (L)	 8,310
JIanville (NU)	 7,534
Strelive (CCF)	 1,993
Campbell (Comm)	 243
These figures indicate that the Prime Minister of Canada was elected by grace of a minority vote of 1,460. I deemed it unnecessary, therefore, to carry my incursion further. I was satisfied to be in the category with the Prime Minister, even if we were only two of a kind.
I am sorry the Prime Minister and the Minister of Justice are not at the moment in their seats. I sincerely hope the Prime Minister has not found too bitter the judgment given on the weakness of our mandates by that great specialist in the art of making statements who sits at his side as his right arm and closest friend. I am sure no one would dispute my right to speak in the house
War Appropriation Bill

on behalf of the electors of Gaspe, and of a large number of those in Quebec who by their votes opposed the government.
The shock caused by the speech of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) when introducing his war appropriation bill of tremendous proportions, to which measure we are asked to give our approval, has occasioned many interesting speeches in the house, and has revived, in the press and throughout the country the campaign toward the formation of a non-partisan cabinet, or a so-called national or union government. In his courageous speech of February 21 the hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot), denounced in no uncertain way some newspapers of his own party. He made a vigorous attack on three members of the cabinet, namely the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston), the Minister of Munitions and Supply (Mr. Howe), and the Minister of Mines and Resources (Mr. Crerar), a unionist of 1917, charging them with being party to the scheme to form a union cabinet.
If one does not ignore the fact that the Liberal government has 185 followers out of a house of 245, and an absolute majority of 125, it folLows that a union cabinet cannot be substituted for the present administration unless pressure comes from within its own ranks.
It so happens that a great number of believers in such form of government are found in the very midst of the Liberal party, with the support of the most influential English Liberal newspapers which, during the election campaign of 1940, were vigorously opposing the principle of national government as advocated then by Hon. Doctor Manion. May I mention here that at a certain conference the Prime Minister, according to a report published by the British United Press, threatened to resign if the lack of confidence persisted.
Moreover, following the hon. member for Temiscouata, the Minister of Justice, speaking in the -house on February 24, said, as reported at page 962 of Hansard:
I do not feel that I could sit in such a government if I were asked to do so and represent my province.
If one compares this statement with the minister's past declarations, he will observe that the minister does not now say that he would fight such a government. Why this sudden neutrality? Since the formation of national government or its equivalent is inevitable-I dare say we will have it within six months-the Minister of Justice is simply preparing his way out. He brandishes before the population of his province this scarecrow
[Mr. Roy.l
of union government, but he refrains from telling the dangers against which he was prone to warn us.
What are these dangers? Could it be the danger of the St. Lawrence waterway project? That danger has disappeared, and cannot, because it is almost a fait accompli, be expected from a union government. Is it the danger of sabotage of provincial autonomy through the adoption by a union government of the recommendations of the Sirois report? If the dominion-provincial conference failed, surely no credit for this failure can be given to the present government; and the danger is not removed if this government is kept in office.
Could it be the danger of unification of railways? The hon. member for Temiscouata gave a pertinent answer to that when he pointed to the special appropriation of 8400,000,000 to be provided for later, to redeem Canadian securities held in England. The Minister of Justice abstains-and the purpose is clear-to mention any of these things he said in the past would come about under a union government.
In this respect, let me quote again his own words. He said:
This mere mention of the name "Union government" brings forth painful memories which it is almost a crime to resurrect at this time.
Here, if I may, I wish to extend to the hon. Minister of Mines and Resources my most sincere sympathy for having received such a hard blow.
What are these things? First, there is the expeditionary force overseas. Three army divisions have already left our shores, and more are to follow. Then there is the national registration. The Houde incident reminds us that we have had it. Then follows conscription. We have had it, too; and I submit that the act providing for the present mobilization of men and resources far exceeds anything done by the union government of 1917. Extravagant expenses? We have a war emergency appropriation of 81,300,000,000, with other commitments foreseen by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) in the budget to be submitted. This will make an approximate total of 82,500,000,000. This parliament will have provided since July, 1940, the unbelievable sum of 84,000,000,000. It is proper here to insist on the fact that, contrary to the usual procedure, we are now having two of these heavy budgets yearly. No one dares to inquire as to the size of the national debt because we all dread the answer. Even before the Minister of Finance submits his budget, our taxes have reached almost the point of saturation.

War Appropriation Bill
We have had war profiteering and squandering. The people are alarmed' and their suspicions are aroused by the government's refusal to allow a public investigation into these vast expenditures. This short analysis brings one to the conclusion that no other government, no matter by what name it might be called, could have gone further. Even with all his eloquence, the Minister of Justice cannot make us forget that. We realize fully that a free, voluntary and moderate war is much more expensive than an ordinary war.
Let me tell the committee the minister's reasons for his pretence of opposition to a union cabinet. They are threefold. The first is that the phantom of union government conveniently serves the minister as a reason for retiring from public life. He knows full well that he cannot hold out any longer against public opinion in his province, nor can he escape the judgment of the trend of events which are turning against him.
The second reason is the fact that a union government would take away from the Liberal party the precious benefits deriving from the exclusive control by the party of radio, the bureau of information and censorship. It would prevent the government from extending its patronage to a certain press in exchange for the praise now showered on the Liberal party. It would put a stop to scandalous patronage in the granting of contracts of all sorts and on such a large scale.
The third reason is: In recalling the union government of 1917-that is the crime, to use the expression of the Minister of Justice-the Liberal party of Quebec is trying to shirk its responsibility. In the face of the inevitable result of their own acts they are preparing to throw the blame upon a union government which they would have themselves already created. In other words, by exploiting the prejudices of 1917 they expect to make the people forget their broken promises and engagements. These are the three true reasons why the Minister of Justice says that he will never be a member of a union government.
The newspapers of the country are justified in trying to end the squandering which shocks public opinion and which is the result of patronage running wild in the granting of war contracts and the distributing of subsidies to jobbers.

speechtext:
I think the Tories are more sincere and logical than the Liberals from Quebec have ever been.
If we keep in mind the supreme object of our war effort, from the state of affairs I have described comes the suggestion of a cabinet so constituted that it would stop leakages,
prevent ruin and ensure a judicious spending of the huge sums which are being exacted from our people for the defence of democracy and liberty. The incompetency and inefficiency of the present government in making good use of public funds are so obvious that I would welcome any change did it not imply the abandoning of the principle of responsible government, the very foundation of the political doctrine we are defending.
Furthermore, it is only right that the party which declared war should see it through and should not be relieved of any of its responsibilities. A few months ago it received a renewal of the expression of confidence of the people, which at the same time was a disavowal of that form of national government. Although the so called King-Lapointe government had never bothered much over whether it had a mandate, had respected or disregarded it, I agree with the Minister of Justice when he says that on account of the unequivocal answer it received to its appeal from the people, the government cannot run away from its responsibilities by consenting to form a union government. However, I condemn the attempt of the Minister of Justice to predispose the province of Quebec against that form of government which may come before long. These tactics of his are dangerous and are bound to destroy national unity. In doing this, the minister who likes to pose as a good apostle of bonne entente and unity is really not giving a good example. This is not the first time this has occurred. Let me quote another instance. During the discussion on national unity on December 3, the Minister of Justice said:
I am not saying anything against Conservatives in the province of Quebec. Heaven knows I would not do that, because they voted for us. They were ashamed of those who were opposing us. That is the reason why my hon. friend, alone, of his clan, is here in the house to-night.

speechtext:
We have listened this evening to considerable discussion with regard to shipbuilding. After sitting here all evening I can quite agree with a remark made in a speech over the radio yesterday by, I believe it was, Mr. Bird, of the Winnipeg Tribune, that the people of the United States were more alive to the fact that there are two oceans, the Pacific and the Atlantic, than were the people of Canada. In an endeavour to bring an important phase of this subject before the government and other hon. members, I wish for a moment to speak about the Pacific ocean and British Columbia.
Sometimes I think that we of the Pacific province are so far away that if we were attacked from the sea it would create no more concern around the city of Ottawa and elsewhere in the east than if the attack were upon Norwray or Timbuctoo. When I heard the leader of the opposition, speaking on behalf of his province, mentioning that ships had been built there of four and five thousand tons, I could not but remark to myself, why are we in British Columbia being neglected when we can build and have built ships there up to 12,000 tons? It may be that during the last war we built ships somewhat hastily, but I agree with the hon. member for Queens-Lunenburg (Mr. Kinley) in deprecating the sale, prior to the war, of our Canadian National

vessels, which at the present time would come in very handily and serve a most useful purpose.
In the last war we did not commence to build ships until 1917, but during the brief remaining war years we constructed in British Columbia something like 135 ships representing a total programme of between 80 and 88 million dollars. It can readily be understood, therefore, that the people of that province are wondering what has happened during this war, when most of the orders for ships have been placed in eastern provinces.
We must take note of both coasts, but I want to touch for a moment to-night on a larger aspect of the subject which was only briefly mentioned by the hon. member for Queens-Lunenburg; that is, the fact that this country of ours is more dependent than any other nation on her export trade by water. Before coming down this evening I looked up some statistics, and it may astonish many hon. members, as it surprised me, that over 60 per cent of Canada's export trade is carried on sea-going vessels; yet to-day and for some years past, Canadian traders who wished to send products abroad must perforce charter ships belonging to foreign nations, and not those of Canada itself.
I am going to leave with the Minister of Finance (Mr. Usley), who, I am glad to see, is in his place to-night, one thought with particular relation to foreign exchange, and I believe I cannot do better than cite what is taking place at the present time as regards shipping on the Pacific coast. We have developed considerable trade with south Africa. Ships running there from the Pacific coast of British Columbia make something like four trips a year. For each trip those vessels take, in freight charges alone, some S200,000, all of which must be paid for in United States funds. I am told on fairly reliable authority that all the costs of our freight on ocean-going ships to-day have to be paid in United States funds. That, it seems to me, is a great loss, and indicates that we are not taking the broad view that we as a nation should with such a gigantic export trade. Sixty per cent of our export trade represents in value well over 600 million dollars' worth of freight a year by water; yet to-day there is not one Canadian ship carrying that freight. Our merchants have to make bargains and charter vessels under foreign flags.
The hon. member for Queens-Lunenburg spoke about the extra added costs. Not long ago we in British Columbia had an example of the control exercised by foreign shipping boards. The poultry producers of British Columbia wanted to ship eggs from that

War Appropriation Bill
province to Great Britain via the Panama canal. Looking around for ships to carry those eggs, they found a vessel of Norwegian ownership which was willing to take the eggs for about $1.85 per hundred pounds. Immediately the "shipping combine" shall I call it, with headquarters at San Francisco, notified the owners of that Norwegian vessel that they would not be allowed to take the eggs at the freight cost they had quoted; that their charges would have to be something like $2.85 per hundred pounds instead of $1.85. Naturally we lost that order for eggs. The merchants and the shippers of this country are in the hands of foreign shipping combines and so have to pay a great additional charge for the carriage of our products to countries overseas.
I fear that, as time goes on, the scarcity of shipping will greatly cripple our trade. Only a short time ago, I understand, the British government requisitioned for her purposes a considerable number of merchant ships which would ordinarily be used in the Canadian trade.
I hope that members of the government, and particularly the Minister of Finance, will view this matter from the broad angle of making this country of ours a maritime nation, not forgetting that we have two oceans, the Pacific as well as the Atlantic. I sometimes think that even in matters of defence we are somewhat like the French, who relied entirely on the Maginot line, forgetting that there were other ways of entering their country and that they should be guarded. The United States is spending hundreds of millions of dollars south from the tip of Alaska, and I do not believe that we are spending as much as we should.
Before I resume my seat I will mention just one other matter w'hich came up in the course of the debate this afternoon. It was referred to by two other hon. members, one of the Social Credit group and one connected with the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation. They were recommending to the Minister of National War Services (Mr. Gardiner) that the forthcoming census be taken on the same basis as that of the national registration, and I gathered the inference was intended that the national registration, done as a voluntary effort-and a splendid effort it was

was done without cost to the government of Canada. If I am wrong in that I am sorry, but that is the impression I got. I find, from looking up the figures, that the cost of the registration will astound even some members who, I know, when speaking privately, express the belief that the national registration last year cost this country but very little, if anything. speechtext:
If we are to do the work on
a voluntary basis, then I suggest that it should be entirely vo'"ntary, involving no cost whatsoever. I know that in my riding- and I suppose other members have had the same experience-there were certain groups who, when the proposal was made to them with regard to assisting, suggested that they be paid for the work called for. The result was that payment was made in one quarter of the riding, while work was done voluntarily in other parts of the constituency, and I know from experience that this gave rise to a great deal of criticism after the registration was finished. I am one of those who believe that if you are going to have the work carried out voluntarily, then the whole thing should be on a voluntary basis. But if you pay some, then you should pay all. I am expressing the feelings of many people in my own constituency, after the experience with the national registration of last year.
Just one word further and I will resume my seat. I have heard it stated on many occasions, and I have heard it again tonight, that there has been political patronage in the matter of contracts. Hon. members who rise in their places and make such statements should be prepared on their word as members of parliament to lay a definite charge or to make a definite statement as to political patronage. I say that in all seriousness. I have heard it time and again, and I know that the inference has gone abroad throughout the country that the government is ladling out political patronage in the face of a very serious crisis of war. I believe every member on this side of the house can say that we are finding it almost a detriment to be on the government side so far as making any approach is concerned, and I can say in all seriousness, from experience, that I have never made a statement on the floor of the house since I came here in 1930 which I was not prepared to substantiate, by naming the particular case. I do not think hon. members should rise in their places and say that the government is handing out political patronage, contracts and positions, for I maintain it is not. I can go further. I do not want to have to do this, but I could do it if called upon. A survey of all appointments which have been made, either in a military way or in connection with the war effort, would show, I believe, a great
War Appropriation Bill

preponderance of those belonging to the Conservative party. I say that in no mean sense for why should they not be called upon to help with the war effort? But I say, in order to controvert statements which some hon. members have been endeavouring to put over, that appointments are not political and that contracts are not being handed out to political favourites.
