speechtext:
I should like
to make one or two observations in view of the fact that there has come to our desks to-day correspondence marked "urgent." Before doing so, however, might I refer for a moment to the observations of the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Reid) with reference to the taking of the census. Is it really so urgent now that war is on? If the national registration did cost money, and if on the other hand we are resolved among ourselves that we will do away with the census for the time being, then it would not cost us anything. At least we would save the cost of taking the census.
After all, what is the census and what is its relationship to affairs as we find them in Canada? The Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston) could tell us how many hundred thousand men are overseas. Will that fact obtain five years hence? We had a census ten years ago. What figures did we use during the interim, in the last ten years? We arrived at our statistics by addition and deduction, and we felt we were reasonably accurate. We have an efficient bureau of statistics, which has received the compliments of similar bureaux the world over, and that department gives us accurate figures. If that is so, if it has been so for the last three or four decades, will not the same condition obtain until such time as this war is over? And would not those figures arrived at in that manner be just as accurate as the figures obtained by a census, should we take one at this time, in view of the ebb and flow of our man-power not only as far as our men going overseas are concerned but internally as well. There is a change in vocation of men and women into different kinds of work, moving from one point to another. City dwellers were asked whether they could milk a cow, and some will go and milk cows; but many more will see these advertisements that the Minister of Munitions and Supply (Mr. Howe) spoke of to-night asking for shipbuilders in the maritime ports, and many will leave the farm. Where will the census be, then, from the point of view of accuracy, in the course of another year or two?
Let us save this $3,000,000, I say to the hon. member for New Westminster. Let that provide 120 Spitfires; let us rely on our efficient

bureau of statistics to give us the statistics we require by addition and deduction; and then, for the man-power we need, let us study the reports that have been tabled by the Minister of National War Services (Mr. Gardiner) and find out where the required artisans are and what is being done so far as their activities are concerned. In the national registration, I say to the Minister of National War Services, we have valuable and vital information. We have that now. Some of the other information we get in a census is only comparative, but comparisons do not hold any longer, because the scene has changed fast since war was declared, and will change much faster while the war is on, from now on, so much so that I am of opinion that it is impracticable, over and above the question of economy, for us to take a census until the Canadian and the world situation settles down a little more than the position of things to-day indicates.
I wanted to say a word or two with regard to the observations of the Minister of Munitions and Supply in connection with shipbuilding. Frankly, I was shocked when I came into the chamber this evening and heard the minister say that the twenty-four hour day has not been employed by artisans in the building of ships since the war started. Not a week goes by when the press does not remind us that Britain's tonnage is some 18,000,000, and that from three to four million tons each year are lost. Indeed, the question is, in view of the strong enemy submarine campaign that is being carried on, how long can we keep up a supply to replace those ships that are being lost? Britain is doing a wonderful shipbuilding work, and has more shipping on the high seas to-day, I understand, than she had at the beginning of the war. But she will continue to do this great work only as we in Canada, Australia and New Zealand, helped by the lease-Iend bill which I am happy to knowr has passed the United States congress, replenish and help her to keep that dominant position which she has had for so many years.
Comparisons are not welcomed by the minister, but I think of that island outside Sydney, Australia, with a six-inch air pipeline twenty miles long all round it with air pressure on ready to serve that greatest of dockyards and shipbuilding yards south of the equator, operated under the direction of the commonwealth of Australia, turning out not only merchantmen that we are speaking about to-night but destroyers, and I think I am right in saying cruisers, as well as aeroplanes, and the men of Australia schooled to take their place in the shipyards doing a real job of work on behalf of the British empire at this time. Where are our schools? Where

War Appropriation Bill
have they been these last five years, that should have been training young men from the farms in the art of shipbuilding?
I had the pleasure of riding into Ottawa to-night with a gentleman who left California last night at nine o'clock, and landed in Ottawa to-night at eight-thirty. He knows the aeroplane industry in California and the conditions in it. Are they closing aeroplane factories at eleven o'clock at night, as I heard the minister say they have been closing the shipyards because personnel to keep up three shifts was not readily available? No. His deposition to me within the last two hours, coming in on the plane, was that they are working twenty-four hours a day seven days a week. And the personnel is being supplemented by young men trained within the last three years in schools so that the aeroplane business can carry on. I do not use that illustration of what is going on in a country that is not a belligerent as showing that they are any better than we are; there are no better people in any line of business than the Canadians. The Minister of Munitions and Supply was told by the hon. member for Queens-Lunenburg (Mr. Kinley) that he had the blood of a Howe. The Canadian people have the blood and brawn. The hon. member -who just took his seat said that in that chart laid on the table here last week by the minister we had a great number of men who were Conservative in thought, and I notice quite a number who are Liberal in thought, but whether they be Liberal or Conservative we have in Canada the brains to do this work. So we have the four Bs, the brains, the brawn, the blood and the bone. Let us then get on with the job.
I do not make this next statement in too critical a sense, but if the administration as at present composed cannot take hold of these virtues of the Canadian people and the great desire in the heart of Canadians to do everything they possibly can in an all-out war effort, then they should sit down round the table and search their hearts in order to see why it was necessary for the Minister of National War Services to rise in his place and say, with regard to the census, "It is not my department; that belongs to the Minister of Trade and Commerce and I do not know about it." Why should this debate go on the way it is doing?

speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
The hon. Minister of Mines and Resources says, "hear, hear." In that regard I will not take lying down any criticism with regard to holding up this debate. Forty hon. members have risen since the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) gave any sort of a summary of what
this vote is about. Even one of his own colleagues who, I understand, should come after him, intervened in the debate; I refer to the Minister of National War Services, the minister of a much junior department and certainly of a much lesser category in respect of the money being spent. His statement came in advance of that of the minister charged with the responsibility of this vote of $1,300,000,000. I should like to have heard, before I participated in the debate, a great deal more from the Minister of Finance. True, he said this should be a matter of question and answer to give him an opportunity to discuss the matter. But when one of his own colleagues rises ahead of him and sets out in detail what he has in mind, and another minister, the Minister of Munitions and Supply, takes the brunt of the debate, what runs through the minds of those of us who have been observing the panorama here for a couple of decades is that it is all lopsided; we seem to be out of order in dealing with this bill.
Another matter which is brought to our attention to-day and which, to my mind, should be at the bottom of the list although it is nevertheless important, is the national salvage campaign. Inasmuch as I have only a few minutes left, I shall reserve my other remarks to another occasion and place a few suggestions on the record with regard to this urgent circular which has just come to our desks. It urges us to think nationally. Of course we should do so, and most of us do. It says we should talk scrap, find scrap, get scrap, help win the scrap and so on. They go on to say that they are going to have a national outdoor billboard appeal, a national newspaper advertising appeal, a supply of leaflets for distribution-

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: More waste of money.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Yes, a waste
of money-a supply of posters for display by local committees, a selection of mats, newspaper advertisements, et cetera, all available in English and- French. There is still time to do what I am going to suggest, but the time is short. First, I make a general Observation, that the cart is before the horse in this campaign. Large municipalities are not headed up with the municipality taking charge. The only way that those in the large centres of population can handle salvage properly is by having the municipality take the leadership and the responsibility for the campaign; then let your propaganda come behind them when they are organized and ready. I will give an instance before I finish. When they are ready, let this propaganda come along and let all these public-minded
War Appropriation Bill

bodies of citizens who are so anxious to do something, such as the daughters of the empire, the local council of women, the veterans' organizations, and so on, across Canada, not do the actual work, which belongs to the street-cleaning departments in large cities, and the health departments in other cities, but urge the citizens to salvage the waste.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: You should qualify for that.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
I can qualify; and, if necessary, I could call a witness to that effect. Let them be properly organized before this propaganda goes out.
I said I would cite an example; that was why I was anxious to take part in this debate to-night. In Toronto we have a very fine body known as the local council of women, who are anxious to help with this work. One gentleman gave them office space; another firm paid for the four or five telephones they had installed. These women, who are familiar with every neighbourhood, set themselves up in their office and received telephone calls from thousands of home owners. But they had no direction. Can hon. members not see how ineffectual it was for them to attempt to operate without some direct contact with the municipality beyond the mayor and board of control saying, "Yes, ladies, we will help you in every possible way. What do you want?" Should the direction come from organizations that are not quite sure of what they want, or should it come from the government to the municipality and then to the organizations?
Before going on with that, let me state what actually happened. Hundreds, yes and thousands of telephone calls were received. The ladies were asked to go to the far end of the city to pick up an old fur coat; they were asked to go somewhere else to pick up a brass ornament, and so on. They hired trucks, picked up all sorts of material, put it in a shed and sorted it. No one knew exactly what they had; no one knew just what to do with it. Another call came in to pick up papers in another section of the city, and one of the girls who were volunteering to drive the trucks, which were hired at so much a day, went to the address and found fifty pounds of old papers. They were brought to the shed, which has been made available by the Toronto transportation commission, and thrown into a corner with other old papers. Then a dealer comes along and offers $3 a ton for everything in that comer, which cost $10 a ton to collect. In this regard I should like to pay tribute to the International Harvester company of Hamilton, which lent a truck for three months.

All through this recital I want to pay tribute to the women who are trying to carry on this work. Their services should be used to encourage people to support this campaign, even as this pamphlet is used for the same purpose; but those who should be charged with the responsibility of doing the actual work are the departments of street-cleaning, which have all the necessary equipment available. How can that be done? In the city of Toronto there are sometimes two hundred trucks on the streets making collections. It would not be difficult for these trucks to carry various receptacles, one for paper, another for scrapiron, another for bones, and so on. The balance of their loads would be taken to the incinerator or the dump, as the case might be, and these receptacles could be taken to the city yard. Then these various commodities could be contracted for and picked up in loads or by the ton, and in that way the work could be made to pay. I think I have made that point clear. [DOT]
How are we going to take advantage of the enthusiasm of these women to see that this job is done? This is my suggestion: zone the	city.	Let the	women sit in	their office,use	the telephone	and see to it	that all thepeople in a certain zone are apprised of the fact that collections will be made the following	day,	and that	they will be	expected toput	their	paper in	the paper receptacle, their
iron in the iron receptacle, their bones in the bone receptacle, and so on. Then, when the collection is made, there will be no delay.
Following that a little further, hon. members must remember that the women who do this work, whether through the local council of women, the daughters of the empire or any other organization, want to get credit for it. Give them that credit. It is a small concession to make in return for the work they will do. They do not want money; they simply want some recognition of the energy and enthusiasm they are putting into this work. I am sony the Minister of National War Services (Mr. Gardiner) is not in his place, but no doubt he will be made aware of what I have said. I suggest that he get in touch with the heads of municipalities at once. In the larger centres do not ask our public spirited men and women to become collectors of rags, bones, bottles, scrap, and so on, at a collection cost far in excess of the value of the material. So much for the situation as far as Toronto is concerned.
I should like to make another observation with regard to the whole country. The great difficulty across Canada is that commodity freight rates are not available on 'the commodities being collected in order to bring them to the point of consumption. Some fifteen

War Appropriation Bill
or sixteen years ago there were commodity freight rates which permitted the movement of many low priced commodities, particularly from the western prairies, to the centres of consumption in Ontario, and that applied also to the products of the maritime provinces. That situation, however, does not exist today, and that is one of the difficulties which must be overcome.
Before resuming my seat, I should like to make one further observation. I think the Minister of Finance has an idea of my views in this matter, which he may convey to the cabinet. The matter of salvage in Canada has to do not only with the civilian population but also with every industry. After all, if industry could cash in on its by-products, very few balance sheets would have red figures. What applies in business also applies to this expenditure of $1,300,000,000. In the organization chart which was given us by the Minister of Munitions and Supply, I looked in vain for any individual charged with the responsibility of looking after the by-products of the industries which are spending this great amount of money. When I think of cost-plus contracts on clothing, shells and what-not, I wonder who is looking after the by-products of those industries; I wonder who is looking after the salvage of scrap metals, borings, scrap aluminum, scrap copper and all the other things coming back from those industries. I wonder whether the cost-plus basis for the sheet of metal which finds its way into an industry also applies when that sheet is punched out and the scrap is left over. I wonder whether we are getting for the Department of Munitions and Supply a full return of the money for the scrap which forms the by-product, coming back from the industry which made the expenditure of the government money in this vote. So much for that class of expenditure.
I come now to the Department of National Defence. I wonder whether the salvage branch of that department is coordinating its efforts with the Department of Finance as much as should be done. I believe, if I asked the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston) or the Minister of Finance to make a statement, we would get the admission that there are some difficulties in connection with getting branches of the Department of National Defence to cooperate to the full in seeing to it that we receive returns from the by-products originating from the heavy expenditures in the Department of National Defence. The salvage branch of the defence department is necessarily a vital one, and what applies to that branch should apply to the whole organization.
To my mind, the revenue from salvage in the Department of National Defence must in its entirety find its way to the exchequer of Canada. I know that is being partly done now, and that it was not done at the time of the last war. I hope the degree of efficiency with which the work is being carried on-and I could elaborate at greater length on that point-has reached a fairly high percentage. But do we know? Is anyone charged with the responsibility of making sure that he knows? Is that person who is responsible definitely answerable to the Minister of Finance who, in the main, is responsible for all moneys coming to the Receiver General of Canada.
Has the Minister of National Defence broken down that right which the army assumes it has, namely, of assuming that what once comes to them is theirs? Is the revenue from by-products derived from stores of second-hand clothing, second-hand boots, shoes, metal, tanks and so on, the property of the unit involved? That condition obtained in England, and I say it should not obtain here. The revenue derived from that source running, as the minister will admit, to an amount of almost $1,000,000 a year, should find its way into the coffers of the Minister of Finance.
I am asking the committee to endorse the idea so that we may reinforce the Minister of National Defence and the Minister of Finance with our view that that which belongs to the government of Canada does not belong to an individual unit. What obtains in that particular should also obtain in connection with all manufacturers doing work for the government. Somewhere within the organization there should be someone coordinating these efforts. The Minister of National War Services should not be left to run his department all by himself, nor should the Minister of National Defence. What is needed to-day -and I am going to suggest it now-is a war-time prime minister who will more and more coordinate the efforts of these hardworking ministers in all departments of government.

This gives me an opportunity just to mention to the committee- and I believe I can do so in two or three minutes-some points which, it seems to me, are not too well understood in the house. I refer to coordination of the war effort.
Let me say this: First, we have a wartime Prime Minister as president of the privy council and chairman of the war committee of the cabinet. On the war committee of the cabinet we have the ministers of the three defence services, the Minister of Munitions and Supply, the Minister of Finance, the Minister of Justice, the Minister of National War Services, the Minister of Mines and Resources, and the Hon. Senator Dan-durand. That body is the body coordinating governmental effort in connection with this war.
May I just in a minute, if I can, indicate to the committee of the house how the committee to which I have referred operates. In the first place we have the three defence services. To some extent those three services are naturally competing in connection with their requirements. The army needs small arms ammunition; the navy needs small arms ammunition, and the air force needs it. So with uniforms, clothing, armaments-so with everything that goes to the fighting forces.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: But is the Minister of National Defence not the head of the three?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
The Minister of National Defence, under the act, is in this position: It is provided that where a particular project affects more than one service the Minister of National Defence, in consultation with the minister or ministers of the other service or services concerned shall make a decision.
But suppose we have a situation wherein the three defence services are in competition. That is ironed out and coordinated first by an inter-service priorities committee. That is a committee composed of representatives of the staffs of the three services, which meets and functions and makes recommendations to the ministers.
The ministers meet in the defence council, which is composed of the three ministers, the three deputy ministers and three chiefs of staff. I do not think there is much difficulty about coordination of the work of the three services. That is one branch of the service. Next comes the ministry of munitions and supply. In munitions and supply you find the

whole purchasing power, not of one service only, as in England, but of the three services- for the navy, the army and the air force. In England we find the minister of munitions and supply purchasing only for the army, and certain raw materials for the other services. The navy does its own purchasing, and the ministry of aircraft production does purchasing for the air ministry.
Coordination is effected in Canada by means of the Minister of Munitions and Supply, who not only purchases for all three Canadian defence services, but also purchases on British account as well. So he has in his charge the full range of the organization of industry in Canada to meet these combined requirements, and has the authority to deal with the raw materials which are needed in connection with that industry.
How is that dealt with? It is dealt with by means of controllers within the Department of Munitions and Supply. There are controllers for the various commodities, who with some controllers in the Department of Labour meet together and form a committee of controllers who coordinate the whole matter of supply and production of raw materials. That is the Department of Munitions and Supply. First we have the defence services; second, supplies, and then third, man-power is to be dealt with.
That is done in the Department of Labour where we have the labour coordination committee, a committee headed by the deputy minister of labour, and composed of representatives, first, of labour; second, of the national labour supply council, which is an advisory body, as everyone knows, representing industry and representing labour, a representative of the Department of National War Services and a representative of the defence services. That brings about a complete coordination and integration among the services in which man-power may be required.
Every demand which can be made upon man-power in Canada is looked into by the labour coordinating committee, and along with that is the national labour supply board, of which I spoke. In the result we have, first, the defence services; second, munitions and supply; third, labour; and, fourth, finance, all tying up in the war committee of the cabinet. With this tie-up in the war committee of the cabinet, headed by the war-time Prime Minister, the blueprint of the war effort of Canada is worked out to the

War Appropriation Bill
highest degree we possibly can; nobody claims perfection because the work to be done changes from day to day and almost from hour to hour.
Before this committee is through, I hope to be able to give hon. members some idea of how the army programme has worked out. My hon. friends of the other two services will give the same for the navy and air. In the war cabinet committee is also tied up the work of the joint defence board. I should have said that the Department of External Affairs is also represented on that committee by the Prime Minister. That department deals with Canada's affairs in so far as they relate to the United Kingdom and foreign countries. I think this is a fairly complete tie-up, a fairly complete integration, a fairly complete coordination of Canada's war effort under men who at least ought to know something about what is being discussed and who are able to bring to this problem first-hand knowledge of the difficulties, the needs and the requirements of the particular services they represent.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: The inspection departments are still under the three branches of the defence department.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: The inspection department has now become a separate board, entirely under the inter-governmental inspection board which is made up of both Canadian and British personnel who give their efforts in connection with whatever may be required. A Canadian may possibly inspect a British requirement or a Britisher may inspect a Canadian requirement. If we have a particular man who can do a certain job on a certain gun, then he does that particular job; if the British have a better man in connection with textiles, for instance, he does that. But it is all done under the one board.

department.

speechtext: Not at all.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: It does not come under the Minister of National Defence; it comes under this joint board?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Not directly under the
Department of National Defence, but under the inter-governmental inspection board, on which there are personnel who were formerly on the department's inspection service.
Progress reported.
